shows.title: The Great Wall of Los Angeles — The 1980s: The Taste of Bitter Fruit
shows.artist: Judith F. Baca and the Great Wall of Los Angeles collective
shows.description:
This installment of SPARC's ongoing presentation of the Great Wall of Los Angeles brings the mural's newest chapter — the 1980s — into the gallery at Bergamot Station. Judy Baca's half-mile mural along the Tujunga Wash is the longest in the world, and this section extends its chronology of California social history into the Reagan era: the rise of Reaganomics and its role in deepening wealth inequality and homelessness, the Free South Africa divestment movement, the War on Drugs and mass incarceration, the emergence of punk, rap and hip-hop as vehicles of dissent, the AIDS crisis, and grassroots organizing by women of color and Central American refugees fleeing US-backed conflicts.

Rather than showing only finished panels, SPARC's Bergamot gallery presentation pairs mural segments with studies, transfer drawings and color renderings, pulling back the curtain on the collaborative, years-long process of building a public monument of this scale. It's a rare chance to see the working materials behind one of Los Angeles's most significant pieces of civic art up close, rather than from a car window along the flood channel.

For anyone who has only encountered the Great Wall as a drive-by landmark, this show recontextualizes it as an evolving, still-growing archive of grassroots memory — one that SPARC and Baca's Great Wall Institute intend to extend to a full mile by the 2028 Olympics. The Bergamot space itself, part of the sprawling gallery complex at 2525 Michigan Avenue, gives the mural room to be studied as art rather than just passed by.

shows.title: Moses@100: A Centennial Exhibition
shows.description:
Marking what would have been Ed Moses's hundredth year, William Turner Gallery has assembled a focused survey of paintings that trace the restless, decades-long experimentation of one of Los Angeles's founding postwar artists. Moses came up through the legendary Ferus Gallery circle alongside Robert Irwin, Ed Ruscha, and Billy Al Bengston, but unlike many of his peers he never settled into a single signature style — the show's selection, drawn from series with names like Roses, Wedges, Crackles, and Waterfalls, makes that restlessness the whole point.

What comes through in these canvases is less a fixed "look" than a working method: Moses treated painting as a physical, almost ritual practice, one he described as trying to be "in tune" rather than in control. He kept at it in his Venice studio until his death in 2018 at ninety-one, and the works on view here — bold, gestural, materially varied — reflect an artist who kept mutating his own vocabulary well into old age.

For a gallery that has represented Moses's circle and legacy for decades, this centennial show functions as both tribute and reminder of how much of today's Los Angeles painting scene still traces back to his example. It's a good one to catch before it closes September 5.

shows.title: Transportation of the Spheres
shows.description:
Dorothy Hood spent decades moving between Mexico City's postwar avant-garde and the wide skies of her native Texas, and that dual inheritance runs through everything in this show. Her large-scale canvases fuse hard-edged abstraction with billowing, cosmic fields of color — dense charcoal or violet voids punctuated by sharp geometric intrusions, as if a piece of Mexican muralism collided with an astronomer's diagram of deep space.

"Transportation of the Spheres" gathers paintings and works on paper that lean into Hood's lifelong fascination with celestial imagery and interior landscape. The pictures often read as thresholds: a dark, saturated ground opens onto a smaller, glowing shape, suggesting portals, planets, or psychic apertures. It's abstraction with a metaphysical charge, made by an artist who talked about her own work in terms of spirit and scale rather than formal problem-solving alone.

Hood, who died in 2000, has been having something of a critical resurgence, with recent gallery and museum attention finally catching up to a body of work that was often overlooked relative to her male Abstract Expressionist peers. This Fernberger presentation is a good chance to see that work up close in Los Angeles, in a gallery space that suits her ambition for scale and atmosphere.

shows.title: Circle House
shows.description:
Oscar Tuazon has spent his career testing the line between sculpture and shelter, and Circle House is one of his most literal experiments yet: a inhabitable structure built from cardboard, wood, and tatami mats, organized around three circles that nod to the enso, the single-brush Zen symbol for emptiness and discipline. True to Tuazon's practice, the joinery and structural logic are left exposed rather than hidden — you can see exactly how the thing holds itself up.

The piece extends ideas Tuazon has explored for years about building as both a functional and a philosophical act: what does it mean to make a room, and who gets to occupy it. Staged as a long-running installation in Morán Morán's Western Avenue space, it gives visitors an unusually long window — nearly the whole year — to sit with a work that's as much architecture as it is object.

For anyone interested in the intersection of sculpture, self-built structures, and contemplative practice, this is a low-key must-see, and its extended run means there's no need to rush.

shows.title: Ongoingness
shows.description:
A gallery-wide group show anchored by Pope.L's "Heaven (Vielmetter Version)," 28 columns of yellowed, stacked disposable plastic cups that reads simultaneously as minimalist sculpture and a pointed reference to Jim Crow-era segregation at public drinking fountains. Vielmetter built the show around that single work, timed to the country's 250th anniversary, and populated it with pieces by nearly the whole roster of gallery artists — Andrea Bowers, Nicole Eisenman, Liz Glynn, Karl Haendel, Mary Kelly, Rodney McMillian, Wangechi Mutu, Robert Pruitt, Deborah Roberts, Paul Mpagi Sepuya, and more.

The connective thread is less stylistic than temperamental: work made by artists processing an unsettled national moment through personal, often laborious means, whether that's Bowers's meticulous graphite rendering of the AIDS memorial quilt in storage or Pope.L's endurance-based sculptural gesture. It's a useful snapshot of where one of LA's most consistently interesting mid-size galleries sees its program heading, and a chance to see a lot of strong individual pieces by artists more often shown solo.

shows.title: Trophies
shows.description:
David Hicks makes ceramics that look like they've been through something. For his third solo show with Diane Rosenstein, the Central Valley-based sculptor fills the gallery with hand-built earthenware bowls, bottles, jars, and ewers whose surfaces have been pushed through repeated firings until the glazes crack, run, and pool like weather damage. He calls the results "trophies" — not in the triumphant sense but as reliquaries for agricultural and floral cuttings, the discarded plant matter of Central California's farmland that most people never think twice about.

There's a deliberate friction in the work between the classical vessel forms Hicks builds and the chaos he then invites onto their surfaces. Titles like Sun Bleached, Red Leaf, and Marigold and Strawberries point to specific botanical sources, but the vessels themselves read as abstract fields of color and rupture — glazes in what Hicks describes as a state of "optimal softening," caught mid-collapse. The effect sits somewhere between still life and geological record.

Hicks has spent his career working at the edges of the decorative and the conceptual, and Trophies continues that project by dignifying the overlooked: agricultural byproduct, roadside scrub, the stuff that gets mowed down without ceremony. Seeing a full room of these vessels together, glazed in wildly different palettes but united by that same cracked, sun-worn surface, makes the case for paying attention to what usually gets discarded.

shows.title: Object Poetry
shows.description:
"Object Poetry" gathers artists who treat sculpture and assemblage as a kind of compressed language, where everyday materials and cast-off objects are recombined until they start to read like verse. The checklist spans generations and temperaments: Bruce Conner's uncanny assemblage sensibility sits alongside Tony Oursler's video-inflected sculptures, large-scale photographic works, and pieces that play with domestic scale and architectural miniature. Across the two galleries, the through-line is a fascination with objecthood itself — the way a chair leg, a lens, or a scrap of fabric can carry more meaning once it's pulled out of use and set into a composition.

Seeing the works installed together across the gallery's two main rooms makes clear how much these different practices share: a belief that objects, arranged with enough attention, behave like sentences.

This is a good show for anyone who likes sculpture that rewards close looking — pieces built from many small decisions rather than one big gesture. It's on view concurrently with a solo survey of Mark Innerst's paintings in the gallery's third room, making a visit worth the time for two very different but complementary shows under one roof.

shows.title: Marilyn Monroe: A Silent Life
shows.description:
Marilyn Monroe has been photographed more than almost any other human being, and this group show at Peter Fetterman assembles the work of the photographers who actually stood in the room with her — Eve Arnold, Henri Cartier-Bresson, Cornell Capa, Elliott Erwitt, Philippe Halsman, Douglas Kirkland, Bert Stern, Sam Shaw, George Barris, Andre de Dienes, Milton H. Greene and others. Rather than the tabloid iconography most people carry around in their heads, the prints here lean toward the quieter, more observational end of the spectrum: Monroe resting between takes on the set of "The Misfits," going over lines in the Nevada desert, or caught mid-laugh at the Actors Studio.

Because so many of these photographers were friends or colleagians of Monroe rather than paparazzi, the exhibition reads less like a celebrity retrospective and more like a study of trust between subject and camera. Bert Stern's "Last Sitting" images, made just weeks before her death, sit alongside Cartier-Bresson's spare reportage from the set of "The Misfits" and Andre de Dienes's early, unguarded pictures of her near Malibu in 1946 — a useful reminder that her image was constructed over more than fifteen years by dozens of different eyes.

Peter Fetterman's gallery has long specialized in vintage and estate prints of classic 20th-century humanist photography, and that connoisseurship shows here in the range of processes on view — gelatin silver prints, platinum/palladium prints, and archival pigment estate prints spanning the 1940s through the 1960s. For anyone interested in mid-century photojournalism as much as in Monroe herself, it's a rich survey of how the top photographers of the era approached a single, endlessly complicated subject.

shows.title: Cordillera Mexicana: Alfredo Ramos Martínez and the Mexican Landscape
shows.description:
Alfredo Ramos Martínez is often called the father of Mexican Modernism — he mentored David Alfaro Siqueiros and Rufino Tamayo and pushed a generation of painters out of the studio and into the landscape. This exhibition, drawn from the artist's estate, gathers tempera-on-paper and oil landscapes made after his 1929 move to Los Angeles, when homesickness for Mexico's mountains and markets became a lifelong subject.

The show's anchor works trace a single mental thread: the Cordillera, the mountain spine that runs from the Sierra Madre down through the Americas. Martínez's Cordillera Mexicana pays tribute to the Sierra Madre Oriental peaks above his native Monterrey, while other paintings place indigenous women bearing flowers and produce beneath the volcanoes ringing the Valley of Mexico. Even his delicate studies of floripondio blossoms — a South American flower he found growing as an ornamental in both Mexico and Southern California — read as a metaphor for his own transplanted life.

It's a quieter, more historical show than most of what's on view in LA's contemporary-leaning galleries right now, but a good one for anyone curious about the roots of Mexican modernism as seen from Los Angeles, a city where Martínez spent his final two decades and where his legacy is held in depth at LACMA and beyond.

shows.title: Yoko Ono: Music of the Mind
shows.description:
Yoko Ono's first solo museum survey in Southern California treats her not as John Lennon's collaborator but as the conceptual artist she was well before the Beatles ever met her: a key figure in Fluxus whose instruction pieces, films, and participatory works helped invent the idea that an artwork could be something a visitor completes rather than just looks at. The Broad's presentation spans seven decades, from spare 1960s text works to the immersive, hands-on installations she's best known for today.

That participatory streak is the heart of the show. Visitors are invited to tie a wish to an olive tree, hammer a nail into a painting, write a note to their mother and pin it to a wall, or add a stroke of blue marker to a boat-shaped sculpture representing displacement and refuge. Alongside these interactive works are historical touchstones like "Cut Piece" and "Fly," which show Ono working through vulnerability, gender, and the body decades before those became gallery-standard subjects.

It's a rare chance to see Ono treated with full institutional weight rather than as a footnote to rock history, and the hands-on nature of the work makes it one of the more genuinely fun, all-ages museum visits in the city right now. General admission at The Broad is free, though the special exhibition requires a timed ticket.

shows.title: California Poppies
shows.description:
Roger Herman has been a fixture of Los Angeles painting since the late 1970s, and this show finds the German-born, UCLA-affiliated artist doing what he does best: turning flowers, mountains, and skulls into loose, saturated fields of brushwork that refuse to sit still. The poppy paintings are the emotional center — layered, almost gaudy stacks of leaf and petal built from dashes and smears rather than careful description — while a companion landscape painting renders a mountain in broad strokes of blue, turquoise, and white.

What makes the show more than a painting survey is the ceramics. Herman throws large, irregular vessels on the wheel and then treats the glazing the way he treats a canvas, letting color pool and shift unpredictably across the surface. A dining table and coffee table extend that same logic into furniture, their tops built from painterly ceramic panels, and a set of tiny mezcal cups modeled on the traditional jicara round out the display at a much more intimate scale.

Pairing an untidy, expressionist painter like Herman with this gallery is a smart bit of counter-programming — proof that the gallery's West Hollywood outpost isn't just showing polished design pieces but also giving space to an artist whose work resists polish on principle.

shows.title: We Breathe the Same Air
shows.description:
Curated by The Pioneers, this group show treats Los Angeles's long fascination with the occult and esoteric — Theosophy, the Krotona Institute, Kenneth Anger's devotion to Aleister Crowley, the Marciano Art Foundation's former-Masonic-temple building — less as subject matter than as atmosphere, something that circulates through the city's art and culture the way marine air does. Rather than illustrating belief systems directly, the works trace how symbols and forms migrate between people, generations, and neighborhoods.

The lineup mixes different generations and mediums: Kenneth Anger's ritual-drenched film work sits alongside Catherine Corman's psychologically charged urban photography, Emma Gray's process-based paintings that let portrait and landscape dissolve into each other, and Jon Pylypchuk's bronze sculptures that turn grief into ghostly, enduring form. Rebekah Rubalcava's paintings work the territory between religious symbolism and feminine sexuality, while Saul Appelbaum's contribution expands past single paintings into a collaborative counter-archive built with several other artists and a text by scholar Susan Aberth.

It's a show more interested in accumulation and coincidence than argument — a loose constellation of LA-connected artists whose work keeps circling similar spiritual and symbolic territory without anyone trying to resolve it into a single thesis.

shows.title: Kinship & Community: Selections from the Texas African American Photography Archive
shows.description:
This exhibition draws on the Texas African American Photography Archive to reconstruct a visual record of Black life in small towns and rural communities across eastern Texas between 1944 and 1984. The photographs are the work of local studio photographers who spent careers documenting their own neighborhoods rather than working for outside publications, and the result is an intimate, unglamorous archive of portraits, church gatherings, rodeos, parades, school pictures, and family celebrations.

What makes the material compelling is its scale and specificity: this isn't a survey of famous images but a deep well of vernacular photography, much of which has never been widely seen and a great deal of similar material from the era has simply been lost. Seen together, the pictures trace four decades that span the height of Jim Crow segregation through the civil rights era, without editorializing — the politics are present in the everyday texture of the images rather than in overt protest photography.

The show is organized by the Center for Photography at Woodstock and curated by Nicole R. Fleetwood, a scholar whose research often centers marginalized visual archives. It's presented at Art + Practice as part of the ongoing five-year collaboration with the California African American Museum, which brings CAAM-organized exhibitions to A+P's Leimert Park space. For anyone interested in photography as community record-keeping rather than fine-art spectacle, this is a rewarding, quietly moving show.

shows.title: The Woods
shows.description:
Dan Mitchell and Richard Sides pair two deceptively plain vocabularies of sign-making: Mitchell's fabricated street and trail signposts, stamped with words like "Boredom," "Gulag," and "Nowhere," and Sides's monochrome enamel paintings, each bearing a single word for a family role — father, mother, brother, stepmother — rendered in a different typeface. Both bodies of work borrow the authority of public signage and domestic labeling, then let that authority curdle into something more ambiguous: directions that point nowhere useful, family names that name nothing beyond themselves.

The show also includes small collaborative sculptures, including a modified microwave mounted on a motorized plinth, and a series of Mitchell's graphite drawings that catalogue the same charged, generic vocabulary — Crying, Molesting, Gossip, Spanking — in a schoolbook hand. Shown alongside its companion exhibition The Cars of Los Angeles, the show sustains Bel Ami's long-running interest in artists who use institutional or vernacular formats (road signs, product packaging, family taxonomies) against themselves.

This is a two-person show for two artists with long, overlapping exhibition histories in London, Berlin, and Los Angeles, and the works reward close, patient looking rather than a quick pass — the wit is dry, and the show's real subject, per its own framing, is the difficulty of finding language and gesture that mean anything at all in an over-mediated moment.

shows.title: Building an Audience
shows.description:
Brad Eberhard makes paintings and ceramic sculptures that feel like pages torn from a private notebook. His works are small in scale but dense with incident — shapes and colors that hover somewhere between abstraction and figuration, built up intuitively until fragments of the recognizable start to surface. For this show, he's gone a step further than usual by hand-building the frames themselves, so that a painting and the object holding it arrive as a single, inseparable decision rather than an artwork plus its display.

The imagery draws from an eclectic private archive: record-collecting, sporting geometry, archaeology, folklore, his son's patterned shirts. Eberhard has spoken about his fascination with Matisse's The Red Studio and its collapse of pictorial space, and about aspiring to the coded symbolism of Jasper Johns and the mystical smudge of Cy Twombly — lofty reference points he treats with a healthy dose of self-aware humor. The ceramic pieces, sagger-fired and glazed, extend the same sensibility into three dimensions, turning everyday objects like sconces into small, strange totems.

What ties the show together is the question posed by its title: can art exist without someone there to receive it? Eberhard's answer seems to be that the making itself is already a form of reaching out, an "oblique diary" that only completes itself in the act of being looked at. It's an intimate, unpretentious show from an artist who clearly enjoys the mechanics of painting as much as its meaning.

shows.title: To Share a Stomach
shows.description:
Organized by Aram Moshayedi with a circle of Iranian curators, writers, and artists as consultants, this group exhibition grew out of an unusual constraint: the works on view were conceived through proposals, instructions, and letters sent by artists living and working inside Iran, then physically realized by other artists and collaborators acting as their proxies. The project took shape in the shadow of specific, recent crisis — daily bombardment and an extended nationwide internet blackout — conditions that made direct authorship and even ordinary communication impossible for the artists who originated the ideas.

The result is less a conventional survey than a study in transmission and trust: what happens to an artwork when the hand that finishes it is not the mind that conceived it. The Brick's installation photographs suggest a spare, deliberately unresolved installation, appropriate to a show built on incomplete information and long-distance instruction rather than finished objects arriving intact.

It's a timely, quietly political exhibition, and it rewards visitors willing to read wall text and press materials as carefully as the art itself.

shows.title: Lorena Alvarez Gómez Solo Exhibition
shows.description:
Lorena Alvarez Gómez, a Bogotá-based illustrator best known for the children's-book series that culminates in her new collection "The Nightlights Collection," returns to Gallery Nucleus with a body of new paintings built around her recurring vocabulary of glowing plants, small creatures, and nocturnal gardens. The show leans into botanical and fungal motifs — mushrooms, water lilies, tangled vines — rendered in the saturated, jewel-toned palette that has made her work a favorite in the children's-illustration and gallery-pop-surrealism crossover scene.

Pieces like "Maleza" (weeds/undergrowth), "Mycena" (a mushroom genus), and "From Decay We Grow" reflect an ongoing interest in cycles of growth and decomposition, treated not morbidly but as sources of quiet wonder — very much in keeping with the world-building of her book illustrations, where tiny stars and mysterious garden spirits populate a child's bedroom at night. Alongside the paintings, the gallery is releasing a set of limited silkscreen prints of individual motifs (Agua, Nenúfar, Marigold, Congo) that let collectors take home single images from the larger visual universe.

Nucleus has hosted Alvarez Gómez multiple times over the past decade, and this show doubles as a launch event for her new book — she is flying in from Colombia for the opening to give a talk on her writing and creative process before signing books and prints. It's a good entry point for anyone curious about the contemporary illustration-gallery scene that Nucleus has built its reputation on: colorful, narrative-driven, and clearly rooted in a children's-book sensibility even as it's sold as fine art.

shows.title: Graven Images to the Major Deities
shows.description:
John Collins is best known around Los Angeles for Moonlight Graham, a daily devotional practice he's kept up since 2019: every night during baseball season, he picks a play from that day's games and renders it in brushwork and ink wash before posting it online. The series now numbers over a thousand works, and this show — Collins's second dedicated to the project at Track 16 — catches it mid-evolution, as he's swapped his original Arches paper for Asian rice and mulberry bark stock that makes the marks looser and more immediate, and ventured into drypoint printmaking for the first time with a set of prints depicting the final games of the 2025 World Series.

The project's charm is in its stubborn earnestness: Collins named the series after Archibald "Moonlight" Graham, the real-life ballplayer immortalized in Shoeless Joe and Field of Dreams who moonlighted as a doctor, and he treats his own nightly ritual — sketching after a day spent working as a handyman — as a similarly quixotic double life. Baseball, for Collins, isn't a subject so much as a structure for daily discipline, a deadline he sets for himself as if filing to tomorrow's sports section.

Outside the baseball works, Collins is known for brooding, autobiographical paintings on scavenged materials — linoleum scraps, chunks of stucco, torn fabric — that read as private ruminations rather than public statements. Seeing both bodies of work together at Track 16, in the gallery's Bendix Building space downtown, makes the case for an artist whose sincerity and repetition are the whole point.

shows.title: 1911 Sunset Boulevard
shows.artist: Marcel Alcalá, Maxfield Hegedus, Kittipong, Arturo Soto, Abdi Taslimi, Evan Whale
shows.description:
Taix French Restaurant sat on Sunset Boulevard in Echo Park for nearly a century before it closed and was gutted for redevelopment, and this show is essentially six photographers and one mixed-media artist working through what that kind of loss looks like. Maxfield Hegedus shot the interior room by room before demolition — bar, ballroom, dining room, both bathrooms, the private room — turning a beloved but unglamorous restaurant into a document of a particular strain of mid-century LA design. Abdi Taslimi's acrylic-laminated photographs of the dining room and the Rhône Room work a similar vein in a different register, more saturated and object-like on their aluminum mounts.

The show nods explicitly to Ed Ruscha's "Every Building on the Sunset Strip," and that reference gives the whole project its logic: this is vernacular architecture photography as elegy, cataloguing a stretch of the city's built environment right before it disappears. Evan Whale's altered c-print, carved and chemigrammed until the image partially dissolves into smoke and texture, is the most physically worked-over piece in the show and a good counterpoint to the more straightforward documentary images around it.

This show uses a single closed restaurant as a lens onto memory, urban change, and the particular melancholy of watching a familiar place get erased.

shows.title: Summer Show
shows.description:
Francis Gallery's first open call turned into a sprawling group show: 79 paintings by 66 Los Angeles-based artists, submitted and juried rather than curated from the gallery's regular roster. The panel — a mix of curators, collectors, designers, and cultural strategists — was assembled deliberately outside the usual dealer-critic axis, which shows in the range of work on the walls: abstraction, figuration, still life, landscape, and everything in between, hung together with more emphasis on variety than a unifying theme.

The gallery's own description of the works gives a sense of the spread — a hovering diamond form in a spiritual composition, a crumpled space blanket rendered with exacting precision in a gilded frame, a circular canvas built from thousands of tiny marks, an interior scene with the loose warmth of an old master painting. Two juried prizes, the Francis Prize for abstraction and the Clara Prize for figuration, each carrying $15,000, were awarded on opening night, named for the gallery founder's parents.

This is Francis's first show with its Los Angeles space as the gallery's sole location, following the closure of its original outpost in Bath, UK last year — making it as much a statement about the gallery's future direction as a survey of the city's painters. Worth seeing for the sheer density of working artists represented in one room, many of whom don't otherwise show together.

shows.title: Focus Female
shows.description:
Focus Female is Leslie Sacks Gallery's fall group show built around women artists working across generations and media — from Alice Neel's incisive lithographic portraiture to Cecily Brown's loose, painterly etching, with contemporary voices like Hiejin Yoo, Amy Cutler, Nicola Lopez, and Clare Woods rounding out the roster. The gallery, long known for its deep inventory of postwar and contemporary works on paper, uses the show to make a case for print and works-on-paper as a medium of equal ambition to painting.

The range on view is wide: Neel's spare, humane lithograph sits alongside Cutler's fantastical, folkloric figures and Woods's boldly graphic screenprints, giving the show a conversational, salon-like feel rather than a single unifying thesis. It's the kind of exhibition where a visitor can trace throughlines between generations of women printmakers without the show over-explaining the connections.

For a gallery built on its editions program, Focus Female is a good entry point — accessible in scale and price, but stocked with serious names, including artists represented in major museum collections. It rewards slow looking at surface and technique as much as subject.

shows.title: Portraits of the Wildly Polite
shows.description:
A group show built around a simple, funny premise: what happens when wild or feral creatures are dressed up, framed, and posed with the decorum of an old-master portrait sitter. The roster reads like a who's-who of contemporary pop-surrealist illustration — Jorge R. Gutierrez (of "The Book of Life" and "Maya and the Three"), Hermann Mejia, Justin Parpan, Brianne Drouhard, and more than a dozen other artists each contribute a piece or two riffing on animals behaving with exaggerated civility: a rooster in formalwear, a fox out for a proper "dog walk," an ermine minding an artist-alley table.

The tone throughout is deadpan-comic rather than cute — these are "portraits" in the classical sense, complete with ornate frames and painterly lighting, applied to subjects that have no business sitting for one. Justin Parpan contributes sculptural pieces alongside his paintings, giving the show some three-dimensional variety, while Gutierrez's boldly graphic, Day-of-the-Dead-inflected animal characters (Rooster Lopez, Don Jaguar, Burro Zebra) anchor the show's more stylized end.

It's a quintessential Nucleus show: playful, character-driven, aimed at the crossover audience between fine art collecting and illustration/animation fandom, and worth a visit for anyone who enjoys seeing a gallery wall used for jokes as much as craft.

shows.title: You want to hear echoes
shows.description:
Leo Mock's paintings read like fragments of overheard conversation — each one titled with a wistful, slightly melancholic phrase ("The stars have grown old," "Pull the smiles inside," "We can pretend we're that") that sets up a small emotional scene before you've even looked at the paint. The works themselves are moody, layered figurative compositions, built up with a loose, expressive hand that leaves plenty of drips, scrapes, and second thoughts visible on the surface.

Presented at M+B's Casa MB space, an intimate, house-like extension of the gallery's main Almont Drive location, the show benefits from close, room-scaled viewing. Mock's palette tends toward bruised blues and warm ochres, and figures often seem to be dissolving into or emerging from their backgrounds, which suits the show's overall tone of longing and half-remembered feeling.

It's a quiet, literary kind of painting show — good for anyone who likes work that rewards spending real time with the titles as well as the images. The exhibition closes September 5, so this is very much a last-chance viewing before it comes down.

shows.title: Kiddos
shows.description:
Matthew Grabelsky is best known for dropping wide-eyed animal-headed figures — his signature mash-up of human bodies and cartoon or animal faces — into the fluorescent-lit purgatory of the New York subway. "Kiddos" narrows that lens to childhood: playground scuffles, temper tantrums, sibling rivalries, and the small dramas of growing up, all rendered with the same uncanny, hyper-real polish he brings to his transit paintings.

The effect is somewhere between Norman Rockwell and a fever dream — technically dazzling figurative painting that uses its animal-headed cast to sidestep easy sentimentality about childhood. A kid mid-tantrum or a "cool kid" in a playground standoff reads as funnier and stranger with a fox or rabbit head than it would with an ordinary human face, and Grabelsky clearly knows it.

shows.title: Take the Bitter with the Sweet
shows.description:
Pony Ma is a Brooklyn-based, Taiwanese-born painter whose acrylic-on-panel works pull from pop iconography and dream logic — cartoonish figures, disembodied smiles, and surreal props arranged like clues in a puzzle that never fully resolves. His paintings favor bright, flat color and graphic clarity even as the imagery underneath stays genuinely strange.

"Take the Bitter with the Sweet" is his second solo show with Thinkspace and gathers eleven new acrylic-on-panel paintings. By his own account the work grew out of a genuinely hard year — a serious injury, a cross-country move, financial stress — filtered not into visible anguish on the canvas but into paintings meant as a retreat from all of it.

The result is a body of work that reads as escapist on its surface but carries real weight underneath: bright, almost storybook imagery standing in for private difficulty, each painting functioning less as a narrative than as a small, self-contained refuge.

shows.title: MARILYN 100
shows.description:
Russell Young's diamond-dusted silkscreen paintings of Marilyn Monroe anchor this centennial tribute, staged in Los Angeles as part of a global program organized with the Marilyn Monroe Estate and Authentic Brands Group. Young, who owns a printmaking press once used by Andy Warhol, works squarely within the pop-art lineage that turned Monroe into an image before she was allowed to remain a person — his high-contrast, glitter-flecked canvases lean hard into that tension between glamour and exposure.

The show pairs new paintings made with access to the Monroe Estate's archive with a broader survey of Young's career-long fascination with fame, celebrity iconography, and the American Dream's underside. Expect large-scale portraits rendered in his signature saturated palettes and diamond-dust surfaces, a technique that makes the images shimmer and shift as you move past them.

It's a commercial, glossy kind of show — closer to spectacle than critique — but that's the point: Young is interested in how fame flattens a person into a symbol, and Monroe remains the ultimate case study. Worth a look for anyone curious how pop art's Warhol-era obsessions get recycled for a new generation of collectors.

shows.title: SPACE IS THE PLACE: Selections from the Hammer Contemporary Collection
shows.description:
Borrowing its title from Sun Ra's 1973 album and 1974 film, this Hammer Contemporary Collection survey turns "space" into a wide-open curatorial question. Rather than a single thesis, the show works through a constellation of ideas — Afrofuturism, migration, domestic space, and the simple, radical act of taking up room in the world — using nearly thirty artists drawn entirely from the museum's own holdings. It's a smart way to make an encyclopedic collection feel like a pointed argument.

The range of material is the pleasure here: Arthur Jafa's charged image-work sits near Betye Saar's assemblage and Fred Eversley's polished resin lenses, while younger voices like Lauren Halsey, Juliana Huxtable, and Danielle Dean push the same questions of belonging and placemaking into sculpture, photography, and video. Thomas J Price's monumental bronze of a Black woman glancing at her phone anchors one gallery with a quiet, outsized authority, and Cauleen Smith's moving-image work threads a more lyrical, essayistic register through the show.

Because this is a free-admission museum presentation rather than a commercial gallery show, there's room to wander and let the connections accumulate — between Nayland Blake's early assemblage and Rodney McMillian's material politics, between Michael Queenland's tiled wall pieces and Arcmanoro Niles's saturated interiors. It's a strong, generous survey of how Los Angeles-connected artists have used the museum's collection to think about space as both a physical and political condition, and a good reminder of how deep the Hammer's contemporary holdings actually run.

shows.title: Through the Sun
shows.description:
Shaghayegh Cyrous builds immersive video and sound installations out of Persian mythology, treating ancient stories as living material rather than historical decoration. Through the Sun draws its structure from Ferdowsi's Shahnameh — the medieval Persian epic — pulling on the story of Siavash, who walks through fire to prove his innocence, and Rostam's trials in the Haft Khan, to build a meditation on passage, endurance, and transformation. Fire and light become recurring thresholds throughout the work: forces that test, reveal, and ultimately renew whoever moves through them.

The show's centerpiece is Bagh (The Garden), a collaged video and sound work combining original and archival footage, staged within the gallery as a theatrical, dreamlike environment rather than a straightforward screening. Cyrous, who trained in Tehran and later earned an MFA in Social Practice at California College of the Arts, has built a career translating inherited myth and oral tradition into contemporary, often site-specific installations — her work has appeared everywhere from Tehran's MOCA to the British Museum to billboards around Los Angeles.

What makes Through the Sun land is its refusal to treat Zoroastrian cosmology and Persian epic poetry as museum-piece antiquity. Cyrous treats the search for light as both a cosmic drama and a deeply personal one, shaped as much by contemporary political and geopolitical pressure as by ancient text. The show runs concurrently with a companion presentation, Breathe the Sun, at Telematic Media Arts in San Francisco.

shows.title: The Development Center: A Clownache Store
shows.description:
For ten days, NOON Projects hands its Chinatown storefront over to Alex Chaves and lets him blur every line between gallery, studio, and shop. The Development Center is a working outpost of Clownache, Chaves's ongoing direct-to-consumer curatorial project that mixes painting with fashion and merchandise, and for the run of the show Chaves is in residence, painting a mural on-site drawn from the geometric, low-slung architecture of early modern Los Angeles.

Alongside the mural, the space fills with new watercolors and a run of hand-produced T-shirts and editions, priced and displayed like retail goods rather than precious objects behind glass. That flattening of gallery hierarchy is very much the point: Chaves treats a hand-painted tee and a framed watercolor as equally legitimate carriers of an idea, and the installation's constant state of in-progress-ness — wet paint, a working easel, product on tables — makes the whole space feel like a stage set for the artist's process rather than a finished exhibition.

It's a small, quick-turnaround show on Chung King Road, the historic strip of storefront galleries in Chinatown that has long served as an incubator for exactly this kind of scrappy, hybrid programming, and it rewards a visit precisely because it won't look the same from one day to the next.

shows.title: New Skies
shows.description:
Severin Hallauer's first Los Angeles solo show builds an entire vocabulary around inheritance — the things, memories, and even traumas we're handed before we have any say in the matter. The Mexico City-based Swiss artist works across sculpture, installation, video, and text, and the pieces here range from intimate to genuinely startling: a modified airline carry-on reworked with cut-paper patterns drawn from Swiss papercutting tradition; a single-frame video confronting a childhood memory involving a gun; and a wall of 355 stained-glass microscope slides, each one tracing a branch of Hallauer's family tree back to 1560, suspended so that moving air makes the slides gently chime against one another.

That installation, Bloodlines, is the emotional center of the show — genealogy turned into both a visual field and a soft, ambient soundscape, memory made audible. A companion piece, Left Overs (Sono stata uui), sets a table with hand-painted ceramics referencing his great-grandmother's floral motifs and embroidered napkins bearing his grandmother's phrase "I was here," treating domestic labor itself as an archive worth preserving.

The show's anchor series, LONG HAUL (i'm only crying on...), takes its title from the specific psychic space of air travel — jetlagged, anonymous, suspended between departure and arrival — and uses it as a metaphor for a life spent between countries and identities. It's a dense, personal body of work from an artist still early in his exhibition history, shown in an intimate gallery space that suits its confessional scale.

shows.title: SURFACE/TENSION
shows.description:
Brooks Shane Salzwedel builds his landscapes the way a draftsman builds a bridge: layer by layer, in graphite, tape, colored pencil, and resin poured over mylar and panel. The results are hazy, backlit scenes — conifer stands, water towers, industrial armatures — that seem to hover somewhere between a photograph, a blueprint, and a memory going soft at the edges. SURFACE/TENSION gathers a new body of these layered works, continuing the LA-based artist's long-running interest in the friction between built infrastructure and the wild land it interrupts.

Salzwedel has spent nearly two decades refining this resin-and-graphite technique, showing from Seattle to Honolulu to London, and the works here extend that vocabulary into new territory. The pieces reward close looking: what first reads as fog or distance turns out to be a literal buildup of translucent material sitting on top of the drawn image, so the "atmosphere" in these landscapes is physically present on the surface, not just illustrated.

At Lola Gallery's light-filled Chinatown space, the show benefits from the room's natural light and movable walls, which let the paintings breathe individually rather than crowding into a single sightline. It's a tightly focused solo outing — a good entry point for anyone curious about the current crop of LA artists working at the intersection of landscape painting and industrial material.

shows.title: The Sound of Gordon Parks
shows.description:
Everyone knows Gordon Parks the photographer — the FSA images, the Life magazine essays, "American Gothic" with Ella Watson posed in front of a flag. Fewer people know that Parks composed music for most of his adult life, writing piano concertos and film scores with the same fluency he brought to a camera. CAAM's exhibition, built with the Gordon Parks Foundation and Parks's longtime musical collaborator Mario Sprouse, is the rare show that treats that second career as a subject in its own right rather than a footnote.

Expect an immersive mix of recordings, video, and archival material — sheet music, correspondence, session photographs — that reframes Parks's visual work as part of a single, continuous creative practice rather than a separate hobby. It's a smart curatorial move for an artist whose photographs are so iconic they can overshadow everything else he made.

For a museum whose galleries sit just off the Coliseum in Exposition Park, this is exactly the kind of deep-cut biographical show that rewards the trip: intimate, well-researched, and focused on an artist whose reputation could easily fill a much shallower exhibition.

shows.title: To Witness Is Never Entirely Passive
shows.artist: Sahab Zaribaf, Ximena Del Cerro, Mary Linda Moss, Mei Xian Qiu, Michal Greenfield, Maria Adela Diaz
shows.description:
Tiger Strikes Asteroid's Los Angeles outpost turns its project space over to a loose coalition of artists, journalists and activists for this six-person show built around a single question: what do we owe the things we witness? Curated by TSA-LA member Fatemeh Burnes, the exhibition treats photography, sculpture, installation, painting and performance documentation as different tools for the same job — holding a mirror up to conflict, migration and injustice without pretending to resolve them.

The roster mixes practicing photojournalists with studio artists, which gives the show an unusual friction. Sahab Zaribaf, an Iranian-born photographer whose images have run through Getty and AFP, contributes press-honed images of moments that resist tidy narratives. Mei Xian Qiu's scroll-and-puppet installation Angel Island revisits the poetry Chinese detainees etched into the walls of the Angel Island immigration station, while Guatemalan-born, LA-based Maria Adela Diaz brings her body-centered performance practice to bear on questions of patriarchy and displacement. Sculptor Mary Linda Moss and painter Michal Greenfield work in more interior registers, using organic materials and portraiture to trace how history and trauma settle into the body.

It's a modest, artist-run show rather than a blockbuster. Worth a visit for anyone interested in how contemporary art is grappling with journalism's crisis of authority and the ethics of looking.

shows.title: 20th Anniversary Group Show
shows.description:
Corey Helford has spent two decades building one of the country's most reliable homes for New Contemporary art — the pop-culture-inflected, technically virtuosic, narrative-driven painting and sculpture that mainstream galleries were slow to take seriously. This anniversary show, the first of a two-part celebration, gathers new work by artists who defined the gallery's program across those twenty years, from hyper-detailed figurative painters to the sculptors and muralists who've made CHG's three-gallery Downtown space a destination beyond the traditional art-world circuit.

What's notable about Corey Helford's roster is how much genuine range sits under the "lowbrow" or "pop surrealist" label: airbrush-smooth portraiture next to gothic fantasy, cartoon-adjacent character work next to fairly serious formal painting. An anniversary show like this functions as a group portrait of that range, with each artist contributing new pieces rather than simply pulling from inventory.

A second edition opens in September, so this first round is really the opening act of a longer celebration — a good excuse to see how a gallery built entirely outside the blue-chip system has quietly become an institution of its own.

shows.title: all the ways to hold tender this land
shows.artist: Anais Franco, Francesca Lalanne, Maddy Inez, Brie Ruais
shows.description:
This group show, curated by Armory Exhibition Manager Danielle A. Hill, gathers four artists whose work grows out of direct physical relationships to land and material — ceramics, steel, wood, film, and even living organisms — to think through memory, ancestry, and ecological repair. It's a quietly urgent exhibition given its framing: the wall text draws on bell hooks' writing about Appalachia to ask what collective listening to land might look like in the aftermath of disaster.

That framing lands with particular weight in Pasadena, where the Eaton Fire of early 2025 devastated Altadena and the surrounding foothills just a year before this show opened. Brie Ruais, whose large-format clay works often record the physical act of pushing and shaping earth with her own body, contributes a video piece here; the other three artists work across sculpture and craft-adjacent processes that treat making as a form of care rather than pure aesthetics.

The show sits in the Armory's Mezzanine Gallery and is accompanied by public programs, including a hands-on Batchelder tile workshop with exhibiting artist Anais Franco and a curator-led walkthrough on the exhibition's closing weekend — both useful entry points if you want more than a quick look at the work.

shows.title: Words Matter
shows.description:
Words Matter gathers seventeen artists from Tierra del Sol's studio program around a single, deceptively simple question: what happens when text itself becomes the material of art? The show turns its walls over to visitors as well — inviting people to write, draw, and tag directly on the gallery walls, turning the exhibition into a growing collective mural over its run.

Among the standouts are Leon Fuller, a longtime Tierra artist since the late 1990s whose text-and-drawing works pull from mass media and celebrity culture, and Joe Zaldivar, whose fictional advertisements mimic real brands while subverting their language. Mary Lou Dimsdale contributes electric, mosaic-toned pieces built from scavenged news text. A sound piece, Exquisite Dream, stitches together studio artists' recorded dream accounts into one collaborative audio work playing in the gallery's Annex, echoing the show's larger interest in voice, collectivity, and what gets said versus what gets silenced.

It's a rare kind of group show — genuinely interactive, unpretentious about its methods, and a useful reminder that outsider and disability-inclusive art spaces in LA are producing some of the city's most inventive text-based work right now.

shows.title: Faces Explained Away by the Light of Day
shows.artist: Exene Cervenka, David Buckingham, Edward Carbajal, Gary Wong, and Cesar Massturd
shows.description:
This Chinatown group show gathers five artists whose work grew out of Los Angeles' underground music, skate, and street scenes rather than art-school pedigree, and the results feel appropriately unpolished and personal. The marquee name is Exene Cervenka, co-founder and singer of the punk band X, whose collages and mixed-media pieces recombine found photographs and scavenged ephemera into small, plainspoken statements — visual cousins to her lyric writing. Alongside her, David Buckingham welds and paints on salvaged desert steel, turning rusted industrial scrap into wall works with a wry, Americana-inflected sense of humor.

Gary Wong, a Chouinard-trained painter who co-founded Gallery 66 in the 1960s and later ran with the Jook Savages collective, contributes layered paintings that fuse his Chinese American background with blues music and California car and surf culture — a long career's worth of cross-pollination distilled into a handful of canvases. Edward Carbajal, a longtime editorial cartoonist for La Opinión and co-founder of the Boathouse Gallery at Plaza de la Raza, shows selections from his surreal, satirical "Mutant Picasso" series, while Cesar Massturd, an Otis grad and founder of the TURD skate/art collective, brings a rawer, punk-adjacent graphic sensibility shaped by East LA street life.

Taken together, the show reads less like a themed group exhibition and more like a loose portrait of a specific corner of LA's creative underground — the overlapping worlds of punk, lowrider and skate culture, and Chicano art institutions that rarely get grouped together this explicitly. It's a solid pick for anyone curious about the scrappier, music-adjacent side of the city's art history rather than its gallery-circuit mainstream.

shows.title: Madonna: The Rise of the Material Girl (1980–1985)
shows.description:
Before "Madonna" meant stadium tours and reinvention as a career strategy, it meant a downtown New York dancer-turned-singer who insisted on writing her own songs and building her own image from the ground up. This photography show pulls together seven photographers — Deborah Feingold, Gary Heery, Jack Lue, Marc Canter, Mark Weiss, Mick Rock, and Richard Corman — who were in the room during those first five years, from club gigs and cassette-tape hustling to the arena-scale Like a Virgin tour of 1985.

What comes through across the prints is less a chronicle of stardom than a document of instinct: Madonna turning down a packaged pop career in Paris to keep creative control, bringing demos straight to New York DJs instead of waiting for a label, and treating her collaborators — photographers, stylists, dancers — as co-authors of a visual identity rather than hired help. Feingold's and Rock's early portraits catch her still becoming that persona in real time, all lace and attitude and un-self-conscious ambition, while Canter's tour photographs from the Universal Amphitheatre show the finished performer arriving.

Musichead Gallery, a Sunset Boulevard fixture built around rock-and-roll photography, timed the show to Madonna's new album and her first partnership with Grindr — proof, as the gallery's curator puts it, that the risk-taking on display in these early pictures never really stopped. For anyone who thinks of Madonna as pure spectacle, this is a useful corrective: a look at the specific, unglamorous decisions that built the spectacle in the first place.

shows.title: WASHOKU | Nature and Culture in Japanese Cuisine
shows.description:
JAPAN HOUSE Los Angeles turns its second-floor gallery over to food itself with WASHOKU, an exhibition exploring the UNESCO-listed culinary tradition of washoku — Japan's rice-and-fish-centered cuisine and its deep entanglement with the archipelago's climate, seasons, and history. Developed with Tokyo's National Museum of Nature and Science and The Asahi Shimbun, this is the show's first presentation outside Japan, featuring natural history specimens, food replicas, historical meal reconstructions, and interactive multimedia rather than paintings on a wall.

The show is organized into five sections that move from a basic question — what is washoku, really? — through the ingredients unique to Japan's geography, a long historical arc from the Jōmon period through the postwar era, the tools and techniques that define the cuisine's precision, and finally washoku's globalization, sushi included. Along the way there are replica meal settings (including a reconstruction of an eighth-century aristocratic banquet from the Nara National Research Institute for Cultural Properties), specimens of fish and vegetables, and archival ephemera like period cookbooks and manga panels.

It's less an art exhibition in the conventional sense than a design- and culture-focused installation. A steady rotation of related talks and tastings makes it an easy, family-friendly stop for anyone curious about the deeper logic behind Japanese food culture.

shows.title: The Sextant
shows.description:
Enrique Martínez Celaya spent decades as a physicist before turning fully to art, and that background shows in the way he treats memory here less as sentiment than as a structure to be modeled and tested. The Sextant is a scaled-down reconstruction of the modernist house his father built on Cuba's coast between 1957 and 1963 — years that bracketed the Revolution, the Missile Crisis, and the U.S. embargo, and that ended with his family waiting there, never able to leave on their own terms. Rebuilding it as an installation lets Martínez Celaya interrogate what such reconstructions can and cannot recover: the piece is explicit about the gap between the model and the real house, between a childhood remembered and a childhood lived.

Housed at the Wende, a museum built around Cold War-era artifacts and ephemera from behind the Iron Curtain and beyond, the piece fits naturally into the institution's broader project of examining how ordinary lives were shaped by ideological rupture. Rather than photographs or archival objects, though, viewers get an immersive architectural surrogate — a dollhouse-scaled stand-in for a real building that, today, operates as a wedding venue, its political scars mostly invisible to the couples who rent it.

What makes the work worth a visit is its refusal to resolve into either nostalgia or polemic. It sits with the discomfort of authenticity questions — is a reconstruction ever equivalent to the thing itself? — while using a deeply personal family story to gesture at the universal experience of utopian dreams curdling into everyday compromise. It's a quiet, contemplative show, best experienced slowly, and it rewards taking one of the museum's docent-led tours if the schedule allows.

shows.title: A Gaze Through Time: Contemporary Reflections on Memory and History
shows.artist: Tahmineh Javanbakht, Shadi Yousefian, Rashin Kheiriyeh, Mohammad Barrangi, Nicky Nodjoumi
shows.description:
This group show inaugurates ADVOCARTSY's new Downtown LA space and gathers five artists of Iranian origin whose work circles around memory as something unstable and alive rather than fixed. Tahmineh Javanbakht's mirror-mosaic wall reliefs draw on the geometric mirror-work found in Iranian shrines and palaces, turning fractured reflection into a metaphor for fragmented recollection. Rashin Kheiriyeh contributes large, richly worked paintings — built up with oil, ink, gold and copper leaf, even espresso — that reimagine episodes from the Shahnameh, Iran's great medieval epic, as a way of asking what old stories still have to say to the present.

Mohammad Barrangi's reverse-transfer prints on raw canvas rework Qajar-era portrait conventions into looser, more contemporary figures, while Shadi Yousefian's collaged panels of actual handwritten letters turn personal correspondence — the residue of migration and family separation — into abstracted, textured surfaces. The inclusion of two paintings by Nicky Nodjoumi, a senior figure known for decades of biting political allegory, gives the show its sharpest edge, tying private memory to the performance of political power.

Taken together the works move between the intimate and the historical, using craft-intensive, materially dense processes — gold leaf, mirror, layered paper — to slow down looking itself. It's a strong first outing for the gallery's new location and a good entry point for anyone wanting a broad, well-chosen sample of contemporary Iranian diaspora art in one room.

shows.title: What Materials Know
shows.description:
Shen Yongji's first U.S. solo show is a study in what happens when an ancient Chinese decorative technique gets rebuilt with entirely modern materials. Working in acrylic, crystal resin, gold, and silver, Shen builds sculptural, light-catching structures out of slices, grids, and layered translucent panels — forms that owe their logic to cuo jin yin, the historic craft of inlaying gold and silver into a surface, but that have none of the weight or opacity of traditional metalwork.

The results read as objects built for looking through as much as looking at: light bends and scatters across their sliced and matrixed surfaces, so a piece changes as a viewer moves around it, shifting between transparency, reflection, and color. That responsiveness to light and to the viewer's position is clearly intentional — Shen is less interested in material as symbol than in material as something that keeps producing new visual information as circumstances (light, angle, attention) change around it.

Here, the inherited technique is a starting point for new sculptural language rather than something being simply preserved or referenced.

shows.title: A Certain Slant of Light
shows.artist: Carl Cheng, Holly Coulis, Tim Garwood, Sky Glabush, Pamela Jorden, David Korty, Aaron Morse, Hubert Schmalix, Sophie Treppendahl, Sung Jik Yang
shows.description:
*A Certain Slant of Light* brings together ten artists of different generations and backgrounds to explore how painting, sculpture, and assemblage can interrogate interiority and personal vision. Carl Cheng, Holly Coulis, Tim Garwood, Sky Glabush, Pamela Jorden, David Korty, Aaron Morse, Hubert Schmalix, Sophie Treppendahl, and Sung Jik Yang each navigate their own visual languages—from Coulis's contemplative still lifes and landscapes to Glabush's evocative gestures, from Morse's engagement with environment and narrative to Schmalix's late works reflecting on color and light.

The exhibition emphasizes how these artists, separated by geography and artistic practice, share a commitment to the picture plane as a site of experiential investigation. Their works resist simple categorization: paintings layer abstraction and representation; sculptures occupy the space between material presence and visual illusion. Together, they pose quiet, persistent questions about how we see ourselves and the world around us.

Drawn from different moments in each artist's practice—some historic works, many recent—this group show celebrates the sustained conversations happening within the gallery's roster, where careful observation and emotional resonance remain central to contemporary practice.

shows.title: Origins of Matter
shows.artist: Hibiscus TV (Amy Kaps and Kaye Freeman)
shows.description:
Amy Kaps and Kaye Freeman have worked together as the collaborative duo Hibiscus TV since 2018, and "Origins of Matter" is the fullest airing yet of their joint practice: paintings, sculpture, hand-built costume and video knitted into one sprawling, maximalist environment. Industrial scrap and cast-off domestic objects get remade into feral, glittering regalia that the two artists then wear in staged performances against room-sized, neon-hot canvases — the show functions less like a static exhibition than an ongoing theatrical residency inside the gallery.

Both artists are past 60, and part of what makes the project pointed is its refusal of any quiet, tasteful late style — instead there's an appetite for excess, color and physical risk that reads as a deliberate argument about what older women artists are allowed to do. Thematically the work keeps circling the same tension: abundance next to scarcity, glamor next to waste, connection next to isolation, using the detritus of consumer culture as its raw material.

Over the run of the show Matter Studio Gallery is hosting three live performance-and-film events (Aug 23, Aug 30, Sept 6) plus a poetry reading, so the gallery itself becomes a stage as much as a viewing room — worth timing a visit to one of those dates if possible, though the paintings and sculptural costumes are on view throughout.

shows.title: Duskborn
shows.description:
Helena Reis's first mini-solo at Copro Gallery gathers six small works on wood panel, each about a foot square, built up with watercolor pencil, watercolor, acrylic, gouache and gold leaf. The Lisbon-based artist paints a private bestiary of hooded figures, birds and half-human creatures rendered in a palette of dusky blues and warm ochres — imagery she's described as balancing something creepy and cute in equal measure.

The small scale and mixed-media layering give the paintings the feel of illuminated manuscript pages or storybook illustrations gone slightly feral. Reis has said the work grew out of turning her own fears and nightmares into something she could look at directly, even find humor in — a kind of exposure therapy carried out one gilded, moody little panel at a time.

It's a quiet, densely worked show, worth a close look on the same visit as Mook Simpson's "America Dreaming" and Dale Sizer's mini-show, both hanging concurrently in the same space.

shows.title: America Dreaming
shows.description:
Mook Simpson paints over reproductions of 19th-century American frontier paintings — Bierstadt, Remington, Charles Marion Russell, George Caleb Bingham — inserting bronco-riding tentacled creatures, alien visitors, and other invasive oddities into the found Western tableaux. The effect is a sly, cartoonish vandalism of Manifest Destiny iconography: the same wagon trains and buffalo hunts that once mythologized the American frontier are recast as sites of strange visitation, undercutting their heroic tone with pulp-comic humor.

The show runs alongside solo presentations by Helena Reis and Dale Sizer in Copro's other rooms. Reis contributes small, jewel-toned panels — gold leaf, oil and acrylic renderings of birds and winged figures rendered with a devotional, illuminated-manuscript intensity that plays well against Simpson's rowdier revisionism next door.

shows.title: Popsicledelic Trip / Pause
shows.description:
KP Projects pairs two Brazilian painters for late summer, each working a very different register of hyper-saturated realism. Rafael Silveira's Popsicledelic Trip leans into candy-colored, almost hallucinatory still lifes and figures — surfaces so glossy and lit they read like renderings of a sugar rush, with titles ("Visual Mantra," "Wonders of Human Nature") that hint at a wry, semi-spiritual undercurrent beneath the pop sheen.

Flávia Itiberê's Pause works in a quieter but equally intense key, built around close studies of single figures and objects — a mask-like face, a wrapped or held object — rendered with the same airbrushed precision but pulled back into stillness rather than trip-like excess. Placed side by side, the two bodies of work argue for hyperreal technique as a vehicle for two opposite moods: one accelerant, one suspended.

This two-hander is a solid entry point into that scene — vivid, technically showy work that photographs well but rewards a slow look in person for the airbrush-level detail.

shows.title: Hammer Projects: Mike Cloud
shows.description:
Chicago-based painter Mike Cloud takes over the Hammer's lobby wall with a suite of oversized, sculptural works that treat the stretcher bar as raw material rather than invisible support structure. His pieces are built from bars configured into geometric and figurative shapes, then layered with oil paint and embedded objects — in this case, children's Halloween costumes and clothing collaged with paper grocery bags, magazine ads and cash.

The centerpiece is a set of three "loosely abstracted portraits," two of them new commissions, hung facade-scale in the lobby. Alongside them are pieces from Cloud's 2007–08 series Painted Clothing, quilted assemblages of kids' shirts and costumes patterned with dragons, fairies and rainbows that read as a meditation on consumer culture's grip on childhood. The clash of soft, familiar materials with the hard geometry of stretcher-bar construction is the show's central visual joke and its central argument.

This is Cloud's first solo museum presentation on the West Coast, and it's a good entry point into an artist whose work sits at the intersection of painting, sculpture and printmaking without settling comfortably into any one of them.

shows.title: Ornélie and Molly Devlin
shows.description:
A two-artist pairing in Corey Helford's Gallery 3, bringing together the French-born painter Ornélie and Los Angeles artist Molly Devlin. Devlin's contribution includes lush, deep-cradled acrylic works like "Fern Echoes," dense botanical compositions rendered with a jewel-toned, almost decorative intensity that recalls both folk illustration and contemporary pop-surrealism.

Pairing two painters rather than staging solo debuts is typical of CHG's Gallery 3 program, which often uses the smaller space to test complementary sensibilities against each other. Here, the throughline is a shared interest in nature rendered through a saturated, illustrative lens rather than by observation, giving the show a warm, almost storybook register distinct from the gallery's harder-edged pop and street-art leaning artists.

shows.title: Case Study: Adapt
shows.description:
"Case Study: Adapt" is the inaugural exhibition at Santa Monica's brand-new municipal gallery, and its subject is urgent and local: how architecture responds to disaster. The show gathers architectural models built by USC Architecture students working alongside ten professional firms, each proposing resilient, climate-adapted housing for families displaced by the 2025 Pacific Palisades and Altadena wildfires.

Rather than abstract design exercises, these are scaled, tangible studies of what rebuilding could look like — homes engineered to withstand fire while still feeling like homes, not bunkers. The project traces back to the Charles & Ray Eames Foundation's original Case Study House program, an explicit reference point for using architecture as a public, optimistic response to crisis.

As the city's first-ever municipal gallery, this space marks a notable civic experiment: using a corner of Bergamot Station's dense private-gallery ecosystem to showcase public-facing, socially engaged design work and pieces from Santa Monica's own Art Bank collection. It's a worthwhile stop for anyone interested in how Los Angeles is thinking, concretely, about rebuilding after fire.

shows.title: the eight directions of the wind: Edmund de Waal at The Huntington
shows.description:
Edmund de Waal is best known to readers as the author of "The Hare with Amber Eyes," but he's foremost a potter, and this yearlong, three-site installation puts his porcelain practice into direct dialogue with the Huntington's own collections. New works appear inside the Huntington Art Gallery alongside historic porcelain and manuscripts, while further installations sit outdoors in the Chinese and Japanese Gardens — a deliberate spreading-out that turns a visit into something closer to a pilgrimage across the grounds.

De Waal's pieces are typically spare: rows of small vessels on narrow shelves, fragments of old porcelain, gold-leafed panels marked with fragments of handwritten text. The material speaks to his longtime preoccupation with migration, memory, and the way objects — a Meissen plate, a shard of celadon — carry histories of movement across centuries and continents. It's quiet work that asks for patience, especially set against the Huntington's more spectacular holdings.

Because it's designed as a yearlong presentation rather than a single show, "the eight directions of the wind" also functions as a slow-release program, with listening sessions and curator talks staged throughout its run — worth checking the calendar for before a visit.

venue.name: The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens

shows.title: Alumni Gallery Exhibition #4
shows.artist: Estefanía Ajcip, Johnny Castillo, Jesse Fregozo, Gabriel Medina
shows.description:
This group show at Art Share L.A. brings back four former participants in the nonprofit's Ellsworth Artist Residency to see what they've made since. Estefanía Ajcip works in fragmented, brightly colored collage-paintings built from old letters and family photographs, tracing the years her father spent working in the U.S. apart from the rest of the family in Guatemala. Johnny Castillo, an oil painter and CSULB grad now pursuing an MFA at Boston University, mines displacement and memory through traditional painting techniques turned toward personal and collective history.

Jesse Fregozo, a native Angeleno, paints the streets and corners of his own neighborhood as stand-ins for identity and inherited culture, while Gabe Medina works in clay, using vessel and domestic forms to explore queerness within family and tradition — a practice that has carried him through residencies from Art Share to Pottery Northwest in Seattle. Together the four artists make a loose portrait of what a residency program can do for early-career, community-rooted artists in Los Angeles.

Art Share L.A. is as much a housing and studio organization as it is an exhibition space — the nonprofit provides live/work space for artists in the Arts District alongside its residency and gallery program — and this alumni show is a useful gauge of that mission's results. It's a modest, unpretentious exhibition, heavier on personal narrative and craft than market polish, and worth a stop for anyone curious about the pipeline of artists coming out of the neighborhood's residency scene.

shows.title: Moth To A Flame
shows.description:
Moth To A Flame is a collaborative installation by the artistic team Kelly Cox and Eric Mullis, who have been making work together for decades since meeting on a high school ceramics field trip in Wisconsin. Now based in Boise, Idaho, the two build environments that sit somewhere between architecture, product display, and psychic space — treating the built world's mythologies, from retail staging to civic monuments, as material to be dismantled and reassembled.

The installation reportedly works through a vocabulary of symbols without fixed answers, favoring sensation over explanation.

Given the collaborative duo's description of the work as responding to "persistent violence and misinformation," expect an installation that's more atmospheric and symbol-laden than didactic — worth the trip for anyone interested in how two people build a single visual language across a decades-long creative partnership.

shows.title: The 35th Annual Exhibition of Korean-American Calligraphy Association: Journey of Ink Fragrance
shows.description:
This annual showcase brings together thirty-nine members of the Korean-American Calligraphy Association for the group's 35th consecutive exhibition at KCCLA, themed "Journey of Ink Fragrance." Calligraphy (seoye) occupies a distinct place in Korean visual culture, treated historically as inseparable from painting and poetry, and this show carries that tradition into the Los Angeles diaspora community, mixing classical brushwork with contemporary compositional choices.

Expect large-scale hanging scrolls and framed works built around ink, paper, and brush — some rendering classical Chinese-character poetry, others incorporating Hangul in more experimental, painterly arrangements. As a juried association show rather than a single-artist statement, the range of hands and styles on view gives a useful cross-section of how first- and second-generation Korean-American calligraphers are keeping the discipline alive outside Korea.

It's a brief, free, walk-in show on the second floor of the Korean Cultural Center, and a good entry point for anyone curious about Korean calligraphy who wouldn't otherwise encounter it in an LA gallery context.

shows.title: Our Beautiful Nature
shows.description:
Galerie Lakaye pairs two very different painters in this two-person show built around landscape and the natural world. Patrick DeCastro's canvases lean into vivid, saturated color and loosely figured scenes — birds, water, foliage — that sit somewhere between observation and reverie, while Simon Edery's contributions bring a more graphic, patterned sensibility to similar subject matter, breaking the natural world into rhythmic shapes and repeated forms.

Seen together, the two bodies of work read as complementary takes on the same premise: nature not as a backdrop but as a set of colors, patterns, and moods to be reinterpreted on canvas. It's a lighter, warmer summer show — a chance to see how that curatorial eye extends to a broader, more international group of contemporary painters.

shows.title: The Shadow Side of Everything – Pt 3
shows.description:
This exhibition is the third chapter of an ongoing painting exchange linking artists across London, Yorkshire, New York, Memphis, and now Los Angeles. Curated by Robert Melzmuf, Christopher Blyth, Karl Bielik, and Rob Hall, it gathers 46 painters whose work ranges from loose, gestural abstraction to tightly structured composition.

The through-line isn't a shared style but a shared commitment to painting as a live, cross-border conversation — each iteration of "The Shadow Side of Everything" has added new cities and new participants, and this LA leg treats the gallery's walls less like a finished statement than a snapshot of an evolving network of studios.

shows.title: Picturing The Arts: Dance, Fine Art, Literature, Music, Photography, Theater
shows.description:
Denenberg Fine Arts, a private gallery dealing in work from the 15th through 21st centuries, has built this group exhibition around a theme rather than a single artist: images that depict the performing and literary arts themselves. The checklist ranges wildly in period and medium — a 14th-century Gregorian chant manuscript sits alongside a Franz Kline etching, a William Hogarth engraving of strolling actresses, a George Condo print of Lenny Bruce, and a Channa Horwitz notational drawing.

The connecting thread is subject matter: dancers, musicians, writers, and performers as seen by artists across six centuries. There's a real range of approaches here, from Hogarth's satirical eighteenth-century theater scene to Willem de Kooning and Franz Kline's mid-century etchings for the "21 Etchings and Poems" portfolio, to Wynn Chamberlain's mid-century figure studies. It's the kind of show that rewards slow looking and a willingness to jump between centuries and continents in a single glance.

This isn't a splashy contemporary gallery show — it's closer to a curated cabinet of art-historical curiosities, priced and available for purchase, in the tradition of the old-school dealer gallery. For collectors and history-minded visitors, it's a rare chance to see this kind of eclectic, connoisseurial hang assembled from one dealer's decades of inventory.

shows.title: Pablo Picasso—Portraits in Disguise
shows.description:
Picasso painted portraits constantly, but rarely in the way you'd expect — he tended to bury his subjects' identities inside symbols instead of showing them plainly. This tight installation focuses on that habit of disguise: a profile hinted at through negative space, a piece of clothing standing in for a person, or one of Picasso's recurring alter egos, especially the harlequin, doing the work of a self-portrait without ever showing his actual face.

Drawing on LACMA's own Picasso holdings, including works promised by Janice and Henri Lazarof, the selection moves across the artist's stylistic range, from Cubist fracturing to the loose, urgent mark-making of his late career. It's a small show but a smart one, built around a single idea — Picasso as a master of pictorial masks — that recontextualizes even familiar-looking Picasso paintings as coded self-portraiture.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

shows.title: Autumn Enchantment
shows.description:
Autumn Enchantment is a large international group show that bG Gallery is hosting at its Bergamot Station space in collaboration with LarkGallery and Vivid Art Studio Gallery, two organizations that run juried themed exhibitions and invite artists from around the world to submit work. The result is a salon-style hang of dozens of paintings, works on paper and mixed-media pieces loosely bound by the idea of autumn as a season of transition — the shift from abundance to stillness, from color saturation to quieter tonalities.
