Because the show was assembled through open submission, the range of styles is wide: sun-drenched landscapes and still lifes sit near abstract color-field paintings, textured mixed-technique works on rice paper, and more expressionistic figurative pieces. Artists in the exhibition work in oil, acrylic, and mixed media, and several pieces directly reference autumnal imagery — orchards, forests, pomegranates and turning leaves — while others use the season more as a mood or palette than a literal subject.

For visitors to Bergamot Station, this is a chance to see a broad cross-section of contemporary representational and abstract painting under one roof, gathered less around a single artistic vision than around a shared curatorial prompt. It's an approachable, salon-hang way to sample a lot of working artists at once before the show closes on September 5.

shows.title: Unlimited
shows.description:
Ji Oh's first solo show at Shatto Gallery gathers years of a genuinely restless, multidisciplinary practice under one loosely ironic title. Rather than settling into a single medium, Oh treats photography, textile, and found objects as raw material to be cut apart and rebuilt: photographs get cleaved and rewoven into new spatial patterns, fabric is dyed and sculpted until it behaves like paint, and salvaged objects get reassigned new functions and meanings.

The show's centerpiece, Light and Spirit, is a large fabric installation that patchworks translucent textile remnants into a quilt meant to catch light the way stained glass does — a fairly literal demonstration of Oh's core move, finding the latent "otherness" hiding inside an ordinary material. It's a smart, tactile show for anyone interested in where painting, textile art, and assemblage overlap, and Shatto's compact Wilshire Boulevard space suits the intimacy of the work.

Coming from a Southern California-based artist with an extensive multidisciplinary history, Unlimited reads as something like a career self-portrait — less about declaring a signature style than showing how many different things a single artistic sensibility can be made to do.

shows.title: tierra
shows.artist: Jackie Amézquita, Natalia Arbelaez, Syd Carpenter, Teresa Castro, Armando Guadalupe Cortés, rafa esparza, Miguel Fernández de Castro, Adebunmi Gbadebo, Karla García, Christine Howard Sandoval, Joanna Keane Lopez, Ruben Olguin, Iman Person, Jeri Redcorn (group exhibition)
shows.description:
tierra is the latest edition of Craft Contemporary's long-running Clay Biennial, reimagined to move past ceramics alone and take in the whole family of earth-based materials — adobe, soil, ash, clay slip, pigment made from land itself. Fourteen Latinx, Indigenous, and Black artists treat dirt and clay not as inert stuff to be shaped but as a living relative: something that remembers touch, labor, displacement, and repair. Joanna Keane Lopez's adobe wall reliefs, rafa esparza's earthen brickwork, and Jeri Redcorn's Caddo-tradition pottery sit alongside newer voices like Miguel Fernández de Castro and Adebunmi Gbadebo, whose material choices carry specific histories of land and labor in the Americas.

What makes the show more than a survey of medium is its insistence on land as archive. Pieces move between grief and stewardship — colonial extraction and border violence acknowledged alongside Indigenous frameworks of care and continuity. The curatorial team, led by Andres Payan Estrada with a committee that includes artist Cannupa Hanska Luger, frames the exhibition as a set of overlapping definitions of the Spanish word tierra: ground, homeland, sediment, ancestor.

For a museum devoted to craft, this is an ambitious swing — using a biennial historically tied to ceramics to ask bigger questions about who gets to claim land and memory through material. It's a worthwhile stop on Museum Row for anyone interested in how contemporary artists are reworking traditional and vernacular techniques into pointed, personal statements about place.

shows.title: The Expanding Field: MOCA's Collection from the 1940s to 1970s
shows.description:
MOCA turns to its own holdings for this survey, using the postwar decades as a case study in how contemporary art actually got that way. Rather than a tidy march from Abstract Expressionism to Pop to Minimalism, the show leans into the tangle of movements that competed and overlapped in the 1940s through 70s, pulling together painting, sculpture, and assemblage from the museum's deep permanent collection.

It's the kind of show that rewards close looking rather than a quick lap: expect the density of a collection exhibition, with lesser-shown works from the vault set alongside the postwar heavyweights MOCA is known for. For a museum literally founded to steward this era of art, this is as close to a mission statement as it gets, and a good primer for anyone trying to understand how Los Angeles's own postwar scene fit into the larger story.

As a collection show drawing entirely from MOCA's holdings, it's a good complement to more thematic, single-artist exhibitions elsewhere in the building, and free admission days make it an easy add to a Downtown museum visit before it closes in late September.

shows.title: Marilyn Monroe: Hollywood Icon
shows.description:
Timed to what would have been Marilyn Monroe's hundredth birthday, this sprawling Rolex Gallery exhibition treats her less as a tragic icon than as a working actor who understood image-making as craft. Hundreds of objects — contact sheets, studio memos, fan mail, wardrobe tests, and personal letters, many shown for the first time — trace how a contract player born Norma Jeane Mortenson built and controlled "Marilyn Monroe" inside a studio system designed to own her image outright.

The costume holdings are the showstoppers: Orry-Kelly's gowns from Some Like It Hot, the unmistakable pink Travilla number from Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, and pieces from the unfinished Something's Got to Give, staged in dramatic vitrines that read as much like couture display as film history. Curator Sophia Serrano uses the wardrobe and paperwork together to make an argument: Monroe's glamour was labor, negotiated scene by scene, dress fitting by dress fitting.

For a museum built around the mechanics of moviemaking, it's a smart fit — less a celebrity shrine than a case study in how a studio-era star authored her own myth. Given the costumes and ephemera on loan, this is very much a look-but-don't-touch show, and worth the wait in line on a busy Wilshire Boulevard weekend.

shows.title: Now We're There (And We' Only Just Begun)
shows.description:
This single-painting installation inaugurates LACMA's new W.M. Keck Foundation Gallery, a space the museum has dedicated to sustained encounters with individual works by contemporary artists. The painting itself, recently acquired by the museum, is vintage Quarles: bodies stretch, double back, and dissolve into one another across a hot, patterned field, the artist's signature warping of line and color making it hard to tell where one figure ends and another begins.

Quarles, who lives and works in Los Angeles, has spent the last decade building a reputation as one of the most inventive painters of the body working today, and this acquisition-and-solo-showcase model gives Angelenos a rare chance to sit with a single major canvas rather than breeze past it in a crowded group show. The tangled, ambiguous figures speak to her long-running interest in mixed-race, queer identity and the slipperiness of being seen and categorized by others.

It's a small show in footprint but a significant one institutionally, marking the start of an ongoing series at LACMA built around deep dives into one artist's work. Free with museum admission, it's worth pairing with the encyclopedic collection just steps away.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

shows.title: Odilon Redon: Otherworldly Visions
shows.description:
Odilon Redon spent the late nineteenth century turning charcoal and lithographic crayon into a private mythology of eyeballs adrift in black skies, cyclopean monsters, and flowers that seem to breathe. This exhibition, drawn substantially from the Getty's own holdings, gathers the artist's noirs — those velvety charcoal drawings that first made his reputation in Symbolist Paris — alongside the lithograph albums and jewel-toned pastels of his later years.

What makes Redon such a satisfying subject for a collection show is the hinge his career represents: trained in the shadow of academic history painting, he pushed toward something closer to the unconscious, anticipating Surrealism decades before the term existed. The Getty's presentation leans into that darkness-to-light arc, tracing how a artist obsessed with disquiet gradually let color and botanical wonder back into his work without ever losing his taste for the uncanny.

It's a quieter, more contemplative counterpart to the blockbuster photography and design shows the Getty has mounted this year, and a good excuse to spend an afternoon with works on paper that reward close, unhurried looking. Free admission, as always, and the show closes mid-October.

shows.title: Life, Liberty, and Los Angeles
shows.description:
The Autry has always been more interesting than its cowboy-museum reputation suggests, and this sprawling group show is a good example of why. Timed loosely around the country's semiquincentennial, "Life, Liberty, and Los Angeles" uses the city itself — its car culture, its immigrant neighborhoods, its protest history, its endless self-mythologizing — as a lens for asking what American ideals have actually meant on the ground in Southern California.

The exhibition pulls from the Autry's deep Western-history holdings as well as contemporary commissions, mixing archival photography, painted ephemera, and new work by living artists. A vintage car painted with a heart on its roof, floating over a faded map of the LA basin, sets the tone: nostalgic and a little skeptical at once, romantic about place without being uncritical about history.

It's a show built for a long run — on view into January — and worth pairing with a walk through the Autry's permanent Western galleries, which increasingly read as a running argument with this special exhibition about whose stories get remembered.

venue.name: Autry Museum of the American West

shows.title: Outsiders, Outcasts, Rebels + Weirdos: Punk Culture 1976–86
shows.description:
It's a little disorienting to find safety pins and Xeroxed flyers in a museum best known for its Jewish ceremonial art collection, and that's precisely the point. The Skirball's punk survey traces the decade between 1976 and 1986 through gig posters, stage-worn clothing, zines, and photography, with particular attention to the Jewish musicians, promoters, and scene-builders who shaped Los Angeles punk from the inside — a history that rarely gets its due next to the CBGB-centric New York narrative.

The show leans into ephemera over relics: hand-lettered flyers for shows at the Masque and the Whisky, cut-and-paste zine pages, and the visual language of a subculture that treated the photocopier as its primary printing press. Cliff Roman of the Germs and other LA scene veterans figure into the accompanying programming.

Paired with the concurrent comic-book survey down the hall, it makes for an unexpectedly countercultural season at a campus better known for Noah's Ark installations and Passover programming — proof that the Skirball's curators are willing to get a little scrappy.

shows.title: f8 Group Photography Show
shows.artist: Cyndi Bemel, Steve Hymon, Richard Johnston, Dennis Lee, Krishna Malhotra, Jim Staub, and Bill Wishner
shows.description:
Once a week for nearly two decades, a small circle of photographers has been meeting in Pasadena to talk seriously about pictures — not just their own, but the history of the medium generally, from old masters to whoever the group happens to invite that week. This show is the public face of that private habit: seven members of the f8 Pasadena Salon, founded by Bill Wishner in 2007, presenting a cross-section of what nearly twenty years of close looking has produced.

Because the show comes out of a discussion group rather than a single curatorial premise, it reads less like a thesis and more like a conversation captured mid-sentence — different photographic sensibilities and subjects sitting side by side, unified mainly by a shared seriousness about craft. It's the kind of show that rewards slow looking, less about any single knockout image than the cumulative sense of a community that has spent years teaching each other how to see.

LA Artcore has operated as a scrappy, community-minded nonprofit in Little Tokyo since 1979, and a photo salon show like this one is squarely in its wheelhouse: modest, unglamorous, and genuinely rooted in the city's amateur and semi-professional art ecosystem rather than its market.

venue.name: LA Artcore Union Center for the Arts

shows.title: Earth Elements: Paint and Fire
shows.artist: Cosmas and Damian Brown, David Lloyd, Gary Brewer, Cybele Rowe, Roger Herman, Brad Eberhard, Cheyann Washington, Xu DaRocha, Marco Minaya, Galia Linn, Aaron Sheppard
shows.description:
Earth Elements: Paint and Fire, curated by painter Gary Brewer, sets out to catch a group of established painters in the act of switching mediums. Every artist on the checklist has spent years at the easel before turning to clay, and the show is built around what happens to a painter's instincts once color and gesture have to survive a kiln. Expect glazed surfaces that read like brushwork, lumpy forms that behave like still lifes, and a general disregard for the old high-craft rules that used to separate "ceramics" from "art."

The premise leans on real art history — the show's own framing traces a line from George Ohr and Peter Voulkos's studio-pottery rebellion through the Bay Area funk-ceramics arguments of the 1970s that Brewer lived through firsthand, up to painters today who treat clay as just another canvas. Cybele Rowe and Galia Linn, both long associated with large-scale ceramic sculpture, anchor that conversation from the sculpture side, while Roger Herman, Brad Eberhard, Cheyann Washington and the rest arrive as painters testing the material for the first time or the tenth.

Eleven artists, one curatorial thesis, and a lot of room to see how differently people handle the same physical constraints. Worth a visit for anyone curious about the current cross-traffic between painting and clay in Los Angeles.

shows.title: Unbound
shows.artist: Ariane Callender, Julia Deckman, Mel Deva, Shelly Floyd, Kyle Goderwis, Ashley Perez, Mark Rebennack, Sarah J.
shows.description:
Unbound gathers a roster of K&K's emerging and mid-career artists for a show built entirely around abstraction — work that has, as the gallery puts it, cut loose from realistic representation to chase feeling through layers, color, and line. It's a fitting subject for this Culver City Arts District storefront, which has made a mission of demystifying collecting for first-time buyers rather than chasing museum-scale statements.

Expect a wall of variety rather than a single unifying style: hard-edged geometric compositions next to loose gestural fields, mixed-media surfaces built up in layers, and color-forward pieces that read as much as mood as image. With eight artists sharing the space, the show works like a sampler platter of where non-objective painting is right now among LA's working studio artists — useful for anyone building a collection who wants to see a range of approaches side by side before committing to one.

K&K keeps its shows on a brisk roughly six-week rotation, so Unbound is very much a snapshot rather than a survey — see it while the paint is still fresh on the gallery walls. The opening reception doubled as an informal meet-the-artists mixer, in keeping with the gallery's low-pressure, "art is for everyone" ethos.

shows.title: Pretty on the Inside
shows.description:
Faidra Koutsouri, who works under the moniker Ghost Girl, fills 7811 Gallery's Melrose Avenue storefront with paintings and mixed-media pieces that treat memory and mental health as a shared, almost tactile terrain. The show's subtitle, "Are You Mental?", signals the frankness of her approach: rather than softening difficult psychological territory into metaphor, Koutsouri renders it in raw, diaristic imagery — dreamlike scenes, fragmented figures, and soft, bruised color that reads as both vulnerable and defiant.

The paintings on view move between intimate self-portraiture and looser, more symbolic compositions, suggesting an artist working through personal history in real time on the canvas. It's the kind of show that rewards slow looking; details that seem decorative at first glance often carry a harder emotional charge once you spend a few minutes with them.

Koutsouri's exhibition offers an unguarded look at how one artist has translated private struggle into a public body of work.

shows.title: Sonsonetes y Menjurges (Tunes and Concoctions)
shows.description:
Avenue 50 Studio opens its fall season with a solo presentation from Rigoberto Soltero, whose Spanish-language title — roughly "tunes and concoctions" — hints at a practice built from mixture: sound, memory, and folk imagery blended into a single visual vocabulary. Given the venue's long-standing commitment to Chicano and Latino visual culture, expect work that draws on vernacular and popular traditions filtered through a personal, handmade sensibility.

Avenue 50 has spent more than two decades as one of Northeast LA's most consistent platforms for Latino and Chicano artists, and a solo show like this one is typical of its programming: modest in scale, rooted in community, and unafraid of bilingual, culturally specific titling that doesn't get diluted for a broader audience.

Located on Figueroa Street in Highland Park, the gallery remains a rare fixture of the neighborhood's original arts enclave, and this exhibition offers a good entry point for anyone curious about the Chicano-art through-line that still runs through NELA's gallery scene.

shows.title: 2026 Student Showcase: Threads of Creativity
shows.description:
Once a year, the Barnsdall Junior Arts Center Gallery turns its two rooms over to the community that keeps the whole operation running: students of the Barnsdall Art Center and Junior Arts Center programs. Threads of Creativity gathers work across mediums and skill levels — from the youngest kids in weekend classes to adult students in the BAC program — into a single group exhibition that tracks the full arc of the center's arts-education mission.

There's no single curatorial thesis beyond the shared experience of the classroom; instead the show functions as an open snapshot of what nearly sixty years of teaching studio art in Griffith Park's Barnsdall Art Park actually produces, medium by medium. Painting, drawing, ceramics, photography, and sculpture typically all turn up in some form.

For visitors, it's a low-pressure, free way to see the park's civic arts infrastructure in action, and a nice complement to the more formal exhibitions across the way at the LA Municipal Art Gallery. Given the venue's mission and modest scale, don't expect polish so much as range and sincerity — which is very much the point.

shows.title: Lotería XII
shows.description:
Cactus Gallery's annual Lotería show turns the beloved Mexican card game into a wall-to-wall group exhibition. Each year the gallery invites dozens of artists to reinterpret the 54 iconic images of the traditional "Don Clemente" deck — El Gallo, La Sirena, La Dama, El Diablito, and so on — in their own style and medium, and for this twelfth edition the gallery has doubled the format, adding a second deck of 54 cards (numbered 55–108) alongside the original set.

The result is a dense salon-style hang of small-format works: oil paintings with gold leaf, folk-art dolls, jewelry, printmaking, and mixed media, each piece keeping the compact scale and bright palette of a real lotería card while carrying the individual voice of its maker. Regular gallery contributors like Fran De Anda, Patricia Krebs, Milka LoLo, and Ilaria Vestri of Disfairy appear alongside newer names, making the show as much a survey of Cactus Gallery's community of women and Latino/a artists as it is a game-inspired group show.

It's a fitting anchor exhibition for a gallery that has built its identity on accessible, collectible folk and outsider art for two decades. Because the works are small and numerous, the show rewards a slow look — spotting favorite cards, tracing how differently two artists render "La Muerte" or "El Corazón," and browsing pieces still priced to take home.

shows.title: Take Your Sweet Time
shows.description:
Scott Hove is best known around Los Angeles for "Cakeland," his long-running walk-in installation of frosting-slathered, faux-confectionary environments that turn sugary kitsch into something a little sinister. For this solo show at La Luz de Jesus, he trades cake stands for clockwork, building a body of new sculptural and wall-based work out of clock faces, gears, and timepiece fragments. The pieces use the familiar iconography of timekeeping to needle at bigger questions about whether time is really the fixed, linear thing we treat it as, or something more slippery.

It's a fitting subject for an artist who has spent his career splicing together things that don't belong side by side — candy-shop cuteness with body horror, mechanical precision with entropy. Expect dense, layered constructions where actual clock parts get embedded in sculpted, cake-like or organic forms, so that the works read simultaneously as functional-looking objects and as reliquaries for a concept (time) that Hove clearly doesn't fully trust.

The show runs alongside two other solo presentations opening the same night at La Luz de Jesus. Hove's clock-crammed constructions should be a good anchor for an evening that also includes new work from Wini Brewer and Susie Ketchum.

shows.title: Some Assemblage Required
shows.description:
Assemblage has deep California roots, and this group show at the California Heritage Museum traces that lineage with an unusual mix of hallowed names and working artists. Curator and executive director Tobi Smith has pulled together pieces by movement forerunners like George Herms and Edward Kienholz alongside Tony Berlant, Michael McMillen, Alison Saar, and Alexis Smith, framing assemblage not as a period style but as an ongoing California habit of turning junk and detritus into meaning.

The show's most visible presence belongs to Chris Fraticelli, a Los Angeles sculptor and former Marine who spent years defusing explosives before turning to art; here he's showing dozens of ceramic works built from salvaged, broken pottery fragments he gathers from flea markets and estate sales. Pieces like "To the Highest Bidder" and "Sealed with a Kiss" rebuild shattered china and figurines into new, often unsettling compositions that comment on consumption, class, and American ritual. It's his third appearance at the museum, and this time the museum is showing a number of works that haven't been on view before.

Housed in the landmarked 1894 Roy Jones House, the museum itself is part of the experience — a Victorian mansion turned exhibition space a block from the beach. Assemblage rewards close looking, and the domestic scale of the rooms makes it easy to get nose-to-nose with the broken plates, found objects, and rusted hardware that make up these works. For anyone curious about the Beat-era roots of California assemblage or just in the mood for smart, weird sculpture, this is a rare chance to see canonical figures like Herms and Kienholz in dialogue with someone still actively mining the same vein today.

shows.title: X Reason
shows.description:
Gronk — co-founder of the pioneering Chicano art collective Asco alongside Patssi Valdez, Willie Herrón and Harry Gamboa Jr. — returns to Craig Krull for his third solo show at the gallery. X Reason brings together paintings, drawings, furniture, mural set designs, and ceramics built around Gronk's recurring vocabulary of black, gestural silhouettes drawn from Greco-Roman archetypes, theater, and myth.

The centerpiece is Conquest, a 16-foot abstract mural spanning four freestanding wood panels, each painted front and back so that spray-stenciled tanks and patterns on the reverse commingle visually with the composition on the front — a device Gronk borrowed from his decades of designing moveable sets for the stage, including his long collaboration with opera director Peter Sellars. Smaller works riff on language and myth: one torso is labeled "Chorizo," another "Echo," after the nymph cursed to only repeat what she hears.

Gronk's career stretches back to the early 1970s Chicano Moratorium era, when Asco's confrontational actions and conceptual interventions (including graffiti-tagging LACMA itself after a curator dismissed Chicano artists) reshaped the conversation around race, protest and art in Los Angeles. This show is a chance to see a living link to that history still working in full, restless force, still finding new shapes for old anxieties.

shows.title: Always the Moon and the Sun
shows.description:
Sebastian Thomas paints like a medieval manuscript illuminator who has wandered into the twenty-first century. His densely worked panels—often bolted together with French cleats so they can be reconfigured into new narrative sequences—borrow the visual grammar of altarpieces, devotional icons, and illuminated books, then repopulate them with sphinxes, warriors, and female saints rendered with a wink toward comic-book pacing and pop-culture irreverence.

The Weisman's presentation, spanning the museum's two-story galleries, gives Thomas room to unfold his mythic tableaux at scale. He mixes his own casein paint by hand, a slow, craft-based process that suits his interest in treating painting as a devotional act rather than a quick gesture. The result is surface work that rewards close looking: gold-toned grounds, jewel-like color, and a density of incident that recalls both International Gothic altarpieces and the crowded panels of graphic novels.

What makes the show more than a stylistic exercise is its cast of characters. Thomas repeatedly centers women—martyrs, monsters, mythic protectors—as figures of intelligence and resilience, using the antique language of saints and beasts to talk about very present-day questions of power and agency. It's a smart, visually generous show for anyone curious about how old forms can be bent to new purposes.

venue.name: Frederick R. Weisman Museum of Art

shows.title: Field Notes from Begumpura
shows.description:
Rahee Punyashloka's installation in the Fowler's Galleria imagines Begumpura — "the city with no sorrows" — a casteless utopia first described in a 15th-century poem by the Bhakti saint Ravidas. The artist casts himself as a speculative ethnographer, producing murals and illustrated field notes that document the invented daily life of this community, from its markets to its rituals of belonging.

The work draws heavily on the visual vocabulary of Dalit and Adivasi mural and folk traditions, using flattened, densely patterned figures rendered in ink and paint to build a world that refuses the colonial gaze that has historically documented these communities. A zine made with the designer Bao extends the project's mythology beyond the wall works, giving visitors something to carry the story home with.

It's a sharp curatorial move for a museum built on anthropological collecting: rather than displaying artifacts of a culture, the Fowler is hosting an artist who inverts the very tool — ethnography — that colonial museums used to catalog and diminish the people Punyashloka descends from. The result is angry, funny, and hopeful in roughly equal measure, and worth seeing alongside the Fowler's other current textile-focused exhibitions.

shows.title: Seasons in Cosmos: Works by Diana Shuiu Wong
shows.description:
This is the inaugural show in the Chinese American Museum's newly expanded gallery, and it's built around one artist's very long view. Diana Shuiu Wong began studying calligraphy and painting in Hong Kong as a small child, later trained in Rome, London and New York, and eventually settled in Los Angeles, where she ran her own gallery in Santa Monica. The work on view spans more than seventy years of that practice, tracking how her abstract paintings have absorbed both classical Chinese brushwork and contemporary Western color and gesture.

The through-line of the exhibition is time itself — Wong's recurring interest in seasons, cycles and the friction between natural rhythms and human disruption of them. Beyond paintings, she folds in film, sound, music and dance elements into her installations, so the show reads less like a static retrospective wall and more like an environment tuned to atmosphere and change.

For CAM, a museum built around telling Chinese American history through artifacts and documentary exhibits, giving an entire new wing over to one living painter's abstract body of work is a notable shift, and a signal of where the institution wants to take its expanded space. It's a rare chance to see seven decades of one artist's evolution laid out in a single museum gallery.

shows.title: ¡AGUANTA!
shows.description:
¡Aguanta! is Dama Gallery's late-summer group show, and the title — Spanish for "endure" or "hang in there" — gives away its organizing idea. The artists gathered here favor visible labor: thick, expressive mark-making, unconventional materials, and compositions that reward a slow look rather than a quick scroll past. It's less about a unifying style than a unifying work ethic, art made by people committed to grinding through difficulty rather than chasing easy resolution.

Installation shots from the gallery show a dense hang of paintings and mixed-media pieces, heavy on texture and saturated color, the kind of work that changes as you move around it and catch different surfaces catching light. It fits Dama's program generally, which has built its reputation on championing emerging and underrepresented artists rather than blue-chip names.

For a Gallery Row space that mounts several exhibitions a year, ¡Aguanta! is a good entry point if you want a snapshot of the gallery's current roster without the pressure of a single-artist survey — a chance to sample a handful of studio practices that share a stubborn, hands-on sensibility.

shows.title: Machine Dreams: Rainforest
shows.description:
Dataland is Refik Anadol's newly opened "museum of AI arts" inside The Grand LA, the Frank Gehry-designed complex on Grand Avenue, and its inaugural exhibition turns an entire five-gallery building over to a single subject: the rainforest, as imagined by a custom AI system trained on more than a billion ecological data points. Rather than framed works on a wall, the show is a sequence of immersive rooms — an 84-projector "Data Pavilion" wrapped floor to ceiling in shifting, data-driven imagery, an interactive "Latent Gallery" where visitors can paint with the model's own tools, a mirrored Infinity Room built around the story of a Yawanawá spiritual vision, and a quieter Sanctuary that turns visitors' own heartbeats into a slowly evolving thirty-foot painting.

What makes the show more than a light display is its insistence on synthesis across senses: scent compositions developed with L'Oréal Luxe, a two-hundred-channel soundscape assembled from rainforest field recordings and the extinct Kaua'i 'Ō'ō's last recorded call, and biosensor wristbands that feed each visitor's physiology back into the work in real time. It's part environmental elegy, part technological showcase, and part theme-park spectacle, and it wears all three modes openly.

Anadol has spent the last decade turning data into large-scale public spectacle, from his MoMA collection piece to his Walt Disney Concert Hall projections, and Dataland is the culmination of that trajectory — a permanent home built specifically for this kind of work rather than a temporary installation. Whether or not one buys the museum's claims about "ethical AI," the sheer scale and craft of the production is worth experiencing in person, and it's unlike anything else currently on view in Los Angeles.

shows.title: Vanished Venice: Ship Cafe + The Annual Venice Canal Festivals
shows.description:
This two-part exhibition inaugurates the Venice Heritage Museum's project of documenting the pieces of the neighborhood's built environment and public life that have disappeared. The first strand, Vanished Venice: Ship Cafe, traces the history of a landmark restaurant and hotel built in the shape of a galleon that anchored the boardwalk from 1905 to 1946, using photographs and ephemera from the museum's archive to reconstruct a piece of the original Venice-of-America fantasy that Abbot Kinney built and that long ago burned away.

The companion strand, The Annual Venice Canal Festivals, assembles photographs and documents from the community archive covering the canal festivals held between 1969 and 1976 — grassroots celebrations that doubled as public declarations of the canals' worth at a moment when their future as a neighborhood, rather than a parking lot or freeway easement, was very much in doubt.

Together the two shows are a compact history lesson in how Venice residents have repeatedly had to fight for and reimagine their own neighborhood, told entirely through the museum's community-sourced photographs and records rather than official archives. It's a fitting subject for a museum that itself only recently found a permanent home, and it rewards the kind of close looking that a small, single-room museum makes possible.

shows.title: Recollection of Communities: A Youth Perspective
shows.description:
This is a student show, and it reads like one in the best sense — earnest, specific, and rooted in real neighborhoods rather than abstract themes. Middle and high schoolers from eight Southern California communities spent a season working with LA Plaza staff and outside mentors on the Smithsonian's Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange program, researching how their own hometowns fit into 250 years of American history. The resulting multimedia projects — the show mixes photography, text, and mixed-media pieces — came out of walking tours of El Pueblo and downtown LA, conversations with archivists and curators, and a virtual exchange with a cohort of students in Baker, Montana.

What makes it worth a visit isn't polish, it's the vantage point: teenagers deciding for themselves which local landmarks, family stories, and neighborhood histories deserve to be preserved. Coming from LA Plaza, an institution built around centering Mexican and Mexican American history that the mainstream record tends to skip over, the exhibition extends that mission to a new generation of narrators. It's a small, free show, easy to pair with the museum's permanent exhibitions on the same visit.

venue.name: LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes

shows.title: Celebrating 50 Years of Art & Community: Selections from the Permanent Collection
shows.description:
For its 50th anniversary year, the Museum of African American Art is turning inward, pulling selections from its own holdings rather than mounting a single guest-curated show. Founded in 1976 by artist and scholar Samella Lewis, MAAA has spent five decades building a collection anchored by the Palmer C. Hayden Collection, including Hayden's John Henry series, one of the notable troves of Harlem Renaissance-era painting in a Los Angeles institution. This year-long presentation surfaces recently donated works, newly conserved works on paper, and archival ephemera documenting the museum's own history alongside the permanent collection holdings.

It's a modest, unhurried kind of anniversary show, more archive-room than blockbuster, and that suits a museum that has always operated as a community space as much as a display space. The current exhibit space sits on the second floor of Baldwin Hills Crenshaw Plaza, where MAAA relocated after its longtime home in the former Macy's building closed for redevelopment — worth noting for anyone who remembers visiting the old space.

Because the show draws entirely from the collection, it changes gradually over the course of the year as works rotate in and out, so a visit in the fall may turn up different pieces than one in the spring. For anyone interested in the deeper history of Black artmaking in Los Angeles, and in Samella Lewis's founding vision for what a museum "for everyone" could look like, this is a low-key but worthwhile stop.

venue.name: Museum of African American Art (MAAA)
venue.address: 3650 W Martin Luther King Jr Blvd
venue.address_detail: Level 2, Suite 283 (inside Baldwin Hills Crenshaw Plaza, across from TJ Maxx)

shows.title: Paul R. Williams: An Architect Considered
shows.description:
Paul R. Williams designed roughly 3,000 buildings over a nearly six-decade career, but this show pointedly skips past his famous Hollywood mansions to look at the other half of his practice: the apartment blocks, garden courts, and low-cost housing schemes he built for Black and working-class Angelenos during the second Great Migration. It's an architecture exhibition at heart, built around more than sixty drawings, photographs, and plans drawn from the Williams archive jointly held by the Getty Research Institute and USC's School of Architecture — perspective renderings in graphite and colored pencil, gelatin silver prints of housing sites, and the kind of working documents that rarely leave an archive box.

What makes it a gallery-worthy show rather than a pure documents display is the roster of contemporary artists commissioned to respond to that material: Edgar Arceneaux, David Hartt, Darell W. Fields, Amanda Williams, Cory Henry, Current Interests, and enFOLD Collective all built new work off Williams's housing legacy, shown alongside archival photographs by Julius Shulman and Janna Ireland. The effect is a conversation across decades — Williams's own optimistic modernism for collective living set against how artists now see the neighborhoods and inequities that housing left behind.

The show is part of a coordinated citywide moment: companion Williams exhibitions open later this year at LACMA and the Getty Research Institute, so the Fisher's version — free, small, and specific to USC's own holdings — is worth catching first, especially for the newly commissioned pieces that won't travel to the other venues.

shows.title: Arthur Grace: WTF? / Jim McHugh: Still At It?
shows.description:
Two veteran photojournalists share the walls of Leica's second-floor gallery this fall. Arthur Grace spent five decades shooting for Time, Newsweek, and Life, documenting American political life (his 1988 campaign-trail book "Choose Me" remains a touchstone of the genre) as well as Cold War Eastern Europe. "WTF?" gathers newer, wryer observational work that turns his reportorial eye on the absurdities of everyday American life rather than the campaign bus.

Jim McHugh, a longtime Los Angeles photographer known for portraits of artists and cultural figures — his image of David Hockney at work in his studio is a well-circulated example — presents "Still At It?", a look back at a career spent photographing the people who shaped LA's creative scene, alongside newer pictures that prove the title's point.

Paired together, the two shows read as a conversation between generations of documentary photography: one photographer trained on the world stage, the other on Los Angeles itself. Both are shown in Leica's dedicated fine-art gallery space above the camera showroom, which also houses the Martin Parr library.

shows.title: Studio Ghibli's PONYO
shows.description:
Four and a half years after opening with a Hayao Miyazaki retrospective, the Academy Museum returns to Studio Ghibli for a show built around a single film: Ponyo, the 2008 fable of a fish-girl who falls for a human boy and upends the tides in the process. The draw here is Ghibli's own donation of over a hundred production materials to the museum's collection — story boards, background paintings, posters, an actual animation desk, and hand drawings by Miyazaki himself, several shown in North America for the first time.

Rather than a dry survey of cels and paperwork, the installation leans into Ponyo's watery, hand-painted world: an interactive animation table lets visitors try their own frame-by-frame sequences, and a play environment aimed at younger guests recreates the film's oceanic dreamscape. It's as much a celebration of the labor of traditional hand-drawn animation as it is of one particular movie, and it rewards anyone curious about what a Ghibli production actually looks like on paper, before it becomes motion.

Curated by Senior Exhibitions Curator Jessica Niebel with Assistant Curator Emily Rauber Rodriguez, the show functions as a kind of sequel to the museum's inaugural Miyazaki exhibition — smaller in scope, but more intimate, focused on the tactile, painterly roots of a film beloved well beyond animation circles.

shows.title: Director's Inspiration: Bong Joon Ho
shows.description:
This is the first exhibition anywhere dedicated to Bong Joon Ho, and it's built on real access — the museum drew on his personal archive for storyboards, research materials, concept art, creature models, props, and on-set photographs spanning his career from early short films through The Host, Snowpiercer, Okja, and the Oscar-sweeping Parasite. It's a filmmaker's process laid bare rather than a highlight reel: sketches next to the finished monster, notes next to the shot.

What comes through is how consistent Bong's obsessions are across wildly different genres — class conflict, environmental catastrophe, and ordinary people pushed into absurd, often darkly funny situations. Seeing the concept art for Okja's genetically engineered superpig next to production stills from Parasite's flood-lit stairwell makes the throughline of his visual thinking unusually legible.

Curated by Michelle Puetz with Nicholas Barlow, the show is a must for anyone who wants to understand how a director who moves fluidly between creature features and social satire actually builds a film from the ground up.

shows.title: Barbie to Anna Karenina: The Cinematic Worlds of Sarah Greenwood and Katie Spencer
shows.description:
Production designer Sarah Greenwood and set decorator Katie Spencer have quietly shaped the look of some of the last two decades' most visually distinctive films — Pride and Prejudice, Atonement, Sherlock Holmes, Beauty and the Beast, and, most recently, Barbie's saturated plastic utopia. This exhibition, closing soon, is a rare chance to see the design thinking behind those worlds rather than just the finished frame: sketches, set photography, and material choices that reveal how a "look" gets built from scratch.

The pairing of Barbie's candy-colored Dreamhouse with the aristocratic gloom of Anna Karenina is the show's clearest argument — that Greenwood and Spencer's real skill is range, moving between fantasy plastic and 19th-century Russian interiors while keeping every choice legible as character and story. Longtime collaborators with director Joe Wright, the two have earned seven Oscar nominations together.

It's a good show for anyone who assumes "production design" just means pretty backdrops; here it's treated, rightly, as authorship.

shows.title: Glow: A Cinematic Moodscape
shows.description:
Glow is less an exhibition of objects than an environment — a two-story immersive installation built around six recurring lighting moods that show up again and again in movies: sunrise and sunset, moonlight, neon, candlelight, fireworks, campfire. Synchronized projections, programmed lighting, and an original score pull imagery from hundreds of films across genres and decades into a single continuous, saturated experience.

The idea is smart precisely because it's so simple: these are the atmospheric cues filmmakers reach for constantly to signal romance, danger, nostalgia, or wonder, and stacking them side by side makes visible just how much of a film's emotional register comes down to color and light rather than plot. It's organized by Associate Curator Dara Jaffe, and it's clearly designed to be walked through slowly, more like a mood piece than a lecture.

Good for a rainy — or blazing — LA afternoon, and for anyone who wants to think about cinematography as sensation rather than technique.

shows.title: 19 Branches of the Academy
shows.description:
A tidy, information-dense gallery about the Academy itself rather than any single film — how an organization that started in 1927 with five governing branches (Actors, Directors, Producers, Technicians, Writers) grew into the 19-branch, 11,000-plus-member body that now nominates and votes on the Oscars every year. A timeline traces how membership categories evolved as film crafts specialized, and portraits of working professionals stand in for branches most audiences never think about — casting directors, sound editors, publicists.

It's a smaller, more archival show than the museum's big immersive installations, closer to a well-made explainer than an art exhibition, but it's useful context for anyone who's ever wondered who actually votes for the Oscars and why categories like "Visual Effects" or "Casting" exist as their own constituencies. Curated by Doris Berger with input from the Academy's own Board of Governors on image selection.

shows.title: Screenwriting: Takes on LA Noir
shows.description:
A compact gallery built around three screenplays, fifty years apart, all set in the same city: Double Indemnity (1944, Billy Wilder and Raymond Chandler), The Long Goodbye (1973, Leigh Brackett), and Pulp Fiction (1994, Quentin Tarantino). The premise is simple and effective — put pages, drafts, and production photos from each side by side and let visitors see how three writers used the same genre and the same city to say very different things about crime, morality, and Los Angeles itself.

It's a script-nerd's exhibition more than a visual spectacle: the pleasure is in the marginalia, the drafts, the small changes between page and screen, and in tracing how noir's hardboiled 1940s conventions got inherited, revised, and eventually blown apart by Tarantino's pulp irreverence. Curated by Assistant Curator Nicholas Barlow, it's a smart companion piece to anything else on view about the mechanics of filmmaking, since screenwriting is the one process here to happen with pen or typewriter rather than camera.

shows.title: Earthen Comforts: Airing Earth
shows.description:
Every summer since 2021, Craft Contemporary has handed its courtyard over to Materials & Applications for a site-specific experiment in public architecture, and this year's installment — the last in the series — is by Liz Gálvez, an architect and UC Berkeley professor whose practice, Office e.g., studies building technologies through an environmental lens. Earthen Comforts adapts passive-cooling strategies borrowed from desert architecture into a set of mass-and-fiber structures meant to shelter visitors from the LA summer without a compressor in sight.

It's a pointed argument against the assumption that air conditioning is the only serious answer to heat: by building shade and thermal mass into the courtyard itself, Gálvez treats climate adaptation as a design problem with genuinely old solutions, not just a technological one. Developed with Berkeley's Wood Lab and thermal consultant Salmaan Craig, the piece sits at the intersection of craft, architecture, and climate research — walkable and shaded rather than purely conceptual.

As the final chapter of the M&A x Craft Contemporary courtyard series, it's worth catching for anyone interested in how museums can use outdoor space as a genuine architecture lab rather than just an entry plaza.

shows.title: Maker-in-Residence featuring Jackie Amézquita
shows.description:
Guatemalan-born, LA-based artist Jackie Amézquita sets up a working studio inside Craft Contemporary for this residency, turning the usually invisible labor of making into the show itself. Using soil solicited nationally through an open call — mixed with masa, cacao, and spring water and sealed with copal — she forms small pebble-like sculptures by hand, freezing batches of earth to "stop time" and then baking them to "activate" it again, a cycle she frames as ancestral and cosmological rather than purely material.

It's a continuation of Amézquita's long-running interest in soil, memory, and ritual as ways of encoding place and lineage, connected here to Craft Contemporary's larger "Untold Story of Craft" series exploring earth, air, water, and fire. Visitors who catch her on site (she's scheduled to appear on select dates through late October) get something rarer than a finished object: a direct, unmediated look at process, with the artist explaining her methods as she works.

Paired with the museum's tierra exhibition and the courtyard's Earthen Comforts installation, this residency rounds out a season-long meditation on earth as artistic material across the museum's whole footprint.

shows.title: Free and Queer: Black Californian Roots of Gay Liberation
shows.description:
This history-driven exhibition makes the case that California, and Black Californians in particular, deserve a bigger place in the story of LGBTQ liberation than they usually get. Rather than starting the clock at Stonewall, curator Susan D. Anderson and her research team trace a much longer arc: Black queer life in California from the early twentieth century through the McCarthy era, the civil rights movement, the AIDS crisis, and on to marriage equality. The material comes largely from archives rather than art-world sources — vintage newspapers, photographs, flyers, and ephemera assembled with ONE Archives at the USC Libraries and community archivists like Lisbet Tellefsen and Alan Bell.

One throughline you can already see in the exhibition's own imagery is the Aché Project, the Bay Area's Black lesbian collective and journal founded in 1989 by Tellefsen and Pippa Fleming — its 1990s demonstration marches appear as some of the show's key images, a reminder that this is protest history as much as it is portraiture. Expect print culture and performance ephemera alongside photography, since the curators are explicit that they're treating publishing and performance as sites of political organizing, not just documentation.

It's a dense, research-heavy show rather than a survey of individual artists, which makes it a good fit for CAAM's history galleries and its mandate to fill in overlooked chapters of California's past. Anyone interested in queer history, civil rights history, or the visual culture of grassroots organizing will find a lot to sit with here, and the show's nearly year-long run gives it plenty of room to become a point of reference for the city's Black History Month and Pride programming alike.

shows.title: Deep Dive in the Archive
shows.description:
Corey Helford's Gallery 2 turns inward with this exhibition pulled from the gallery's own back rooms, resurfacing works by artists in its stable that have not been on public view in years. Rather than a single-artist survey, it operates like a cabinet of curiosities from two decades of the gallery's program, letting visitors trace throughlines between the pop-surrealist and lowbrow-adjacent painters CHG has championed since its founding.

Shows built from archives are as much about a gallery's institutional memory as they are about any one artist, and that's the appeal here: a chance to see how CHG's identity has shifted (or held steady) since it opened in the Arts District two decades ago, presented alongside its 20th Anniversary exhibition in the main gallery this same month.

shows.title: Things I Like
shows.description:
Patrick Wilson makes hard-edge abstract paintings the slow way: dozens of ultra-thin, translucent and opaque films of acrylic pulled across the canvas in careful sequence, each color decision keyed to the one before it. The results are geometric compositions that read as flat and luminous at once, with titles like "Free Lemons" and "Szechuan Food" arrived at through free association after the paintings are finished rather than as illustrative starting points.

There's a distinctly Southern Californian light in Wilson's palette — acid yellows, sky blues, marmalade orange, hot pink against teal — that places him in a lineage of LA hard-edge and Light and Space painting without simply repeating it. The appeal of the work is in its insistence on slowness: in an image-saturated moment, Wilson is making paintings that only give up their structure to someone willing to actually stand and look.

shows.title: Paint, oil, water
shows.description:
Ann Thornycroft has been painting in Los Angeles since arriving from London and New York in the early 1970s, and this show gathers a year's worth of new abstractions built on the grid she has spent decades refining. Each canvas starts from a twelve-inch square lattice, sometimes barely visible as pencil beneath washes of poured pigment, sometimes broken into rounded triangular and vesica-shaped units that recall quilting and Pattern & Decoration painting without ever tipping into its maximalism.

What distinguishes the new work is how much further the paint has been allowed to take over. In a piece like Ancient Glass, sea-foam greens and blues churn across the canvas, all but dissolving the underlying structure into pure atmosphere. That push between the rational scaffold of the grid and the loose, wet unpredictability of poured color has always been Thornycroft's subject, and here the balance tips toward openness and vulnerability rather than the earlier control.

Thornycroft's career threads through Venice Beach's Light and Space scene (Robert Irwin once helped her secure an NEA grant) and decades of Los Angeles gallery history, without ever locking into one movement's orthodoxy. This is a chance to see a veteran abstract painter still actively pushing her own vocabulary rather than repeating it.

shows.title: Anteroom: Growing by Living Together
shows.description:
Sarah Ippolito is a scuba diver as much as a sculptor, and this small presentation in Official Welcome's Anteroom space translates that underwater looking into ceramic, wood, and metal. Two new tondos take the round format's long history — Roman shields, deschi da parto, ecology diagrams — and use it to compress the feeling of facing a coral reef wall: a dense, teeming, close-up superorganism where everything grows because it grows together.

Alongside the tondos, a large wall-mounted sculpture isolates a single plane from Ippolito's freestanding work, letting a biomorphic form hang free of the ground the way a creature might drift in open water. The palette and texture throughout lean toward the neon and crackling colors of reef life rather than any tasteful marine blue, which is the point: Ippolito treats ocean biodiversity as a subject for genuine sensory immersion rather than pretty reference.

Houston-born and now Altadena-based, Ippolito has shown at Various Small Fires and the A+D Museum, and her work carries a scientist's curiosity about nonhuman embodiment alongside a sculptor's feel for material. This is a compact but vivid entry point into a practice built on empathy for creatures most of us never get close to.

shows.title: SMOL 3.0
shows.dates_note: page's exhibition-archive header lists Aug 8 - Sept 5, 2026, though the show's own body text mentions an earlier Aug 29 close for a prior edition; going with the header dates as current
shows.description:
SMOL is Thinkspace's annual survey of small-scale work — everything on view is 12x16 inches or under — pitched as an approachable entry point for new collectors and a chance for longtime gallery artists to show something looser and less precious than a full solo body of work.

The 2026 edition, SMOL 3.0, is a genuinely sprawling group show: roughly fifty artists from the gallery's roster are included, spanning painters and illustrators working across the New Contemporary spectrum, from pop-surrealist figuration to graffiti-adjacent abstraction. Names range from gallery mainstays like Kelly Vivanco, Fumi Nakamura's stylistic peers, and KOLA DPW to muralists and printmakers who don't often get wall space in a group context this democratic.

It's less a curated thesis than a salon-style hang, and that's the point — visitors can find a manageable, collectible piece from an artist whose larger work they might otherwise only see in a museum-scale mural or a five-figure canvas.

shows.title: Spotlight on Local Creatives (with Roger Betka | Jordan Tacker | Juri Umagami)
shows.artist: Roger Betka, Jordan Tacker, Juri Umagami
shows.description:
Session Sixteen of Thinkspace's Fresh Series, curated by Cannibal Flower, spotlights three Los Angeles-area artists — Roger Betka, Jordan Tacker, and Juri Umagami — in a compact group showcase running alongside the gallery's bigger solo exhibitions.

The series exists specifically to give local, often earlier-career artists gallery wall space without waiting for a full solo slot, and each session functions more as an introduction than a thesis show — a rotating snapshot of names worth watching in LA's current scene.

It runs through September 5 in the gallery's West Adams space, concurrent with Pony Ma's and Matthew Grabelsky's solo shows.

shows.title: Anton Roland Laub: Mobile Churches in Ceaușescu's Bucharest
shows.description:
In the 1980s, Nicolae Ceaușescu's "systematization" campaign flattened roughly a third of historic Bucharest to make way for the oversized avenues and government buildings of a totalitarian regime. Seven churches, deemed too significant to destroy outright, were instead jacked up, set on rails, and physically wheeled behind new apartment blocks — hidden in plain sight rather than demolished. Photographer Anton Roland Laub, who grew up amid this leveled cityscape, spent years tracking down these displaced structures and documenting how they sit today, wedged into gaps between mismatched postwar architecture.

The exhibition — Laub's first solo presentation in the United States — pairs his contemporary large-format photographs with archival material from the era of the relocations, including material from the engineer who devised the rail-lifting technique. The pictures are quiet and procedural rather than sensational: facades caught at odd angles against concrete housing, empty lots where history was erased, buildings that look stranded rather than saved. Together they form a document of a strange, little-known act of architectural survival under one of Eastern Europe's most destructive dictatorships.

This is the first chapter of a three-part project by Laub examining the final years of the Ceaușescu regime, continued in his later series Last Christmas (of Ceaușescu) and Mineriada. Guest-curated by independent curator Sonia Voss, the show rewards a slow look at how state power reshapes — and sometimes just relocates — the physical fabric of a city.

shows.title: Ivana Dama: Breathing Alarms
shows.description:
Tucked into the East German guardhouse that sits in the Wende's sculpture garden, this installation by Belgrade-born, New York-based artist Ivana Dama turns a Cold War-era surveillance structure into an instrument that visitors themselves have to play. At its center is a custom air-raid siren — historically a device that broadcasts danger to a passive public — rebuilt here so that it only sounds when someone breathes into it. That breath simultaneously spins a small aluminum zoetrope showing an animation of birds, so the piece links two very different alarm systems: the mechanical siren and the natural, and increasingly threatened, phenomenon of birdsong.

Dama developed the piece's mechanics with researchers at MIT's Center for Bits and Atoms, and the result is deceptively simple to encounter even though the engineering behind it is intricate. Rather than a spectacle, it's a quiet, participatory gesture: visitors have to lean in and exhale to make anything happen at all, turning a device built for collective alarm into something that depends on individual, bodily presence.

The work fits the guardhouse's ongoing role at the Wende as a rotating site for artists responding to themes of surveillance, borders, and state power, and it extends Dama's longer-running research into sirens and warning systems, drawing a line between the sound of Cold War civil defense and her own memories of the bombing of Belgrade in 1999.

shows.title: Group Exhibition of Abstract Work
shows.description:
Not There closes out the summer with a straightforwardly titled group show built entirely around abstraction — a chance to see how a roster of artists working outside representational imagery handle color, gesture, and surface differently from one another. Given the gallery's mission of opening its Chinatown walls to under-represented artists, expect the checklist to skew toward names you won't already know from the bigger Chinatown or Culver City spaces.

Judging from the installation photography the gallery has posted, the show favors large-scale canvases hung salon-style against the gallery's raw walls, with plenty of texture — layered paint, torn and reworked surfaces, and some pieces that push into collage and mixed media. It's the kind of show that rewards wandering rather than a single guided read.

Not There has built a strong run of solo and two-artist shows in its small Gin Ling Way space over the past few years; this group format is a departure that lets the gallery show its range across several practices at once before the space cycles into its next solo commitment.

shows.title: Eileen Cowin: Between Panic and Paradise
shows.description:
Eileen Cowin has spent five decades staging photographs and videos that look like scenes from movies you never quite saw — domestic dramas full of glances, standoffs, and unresolved tension between the people in them. This survey pulls together her experimental photographic processes, Polaroids, inkjet prints, and video work, much of it drawn from LACMA's own holdings and other Southern California museum collections, to trace how she has used cinema, literature, and painting as source material for pictures that hover between document and fiction.

What makes Cowin's work stand out among her Pictures Generation contemporaries is how personal and specifically Los Angeles it feels — the light, the domestic interiors, the sense of a life being narrated in fragments. Seeing this much of her output together offers a rare chance to track how her interest in doubling, rivalry, and role-play has evolved across changing photographic technologies, from analog Polaroids to digital video.

This is a show for anyone interested in how photography can borrow the grammar of film and theater without ever fully committing to a plot — Cowin leaves just enough ambiguity that every image reads as a still from a story you have to invent yourself.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

shows.title: Fashioning Chinese Women: Empire to Modernity
shows.description:
More than seventy garments trace a century of change in Chinese women's dress, moving from the loose embroidered robes of the late Qing court through the fitted 1930s qipao to the cheongsam that became a global fashion icon by the 1960s. Drawn largely from Shanghai, Hong Kong, and Chinese American wardrobes, the pieces on view are less about fashion history in the abstract than about the women who wore them — how cut, fabric, and silhouette became ways of signaling identity through decades of political and social upheaval.

The mannequins themselves are part of the story: designer Jason Wu customized the forms specifically for this installation, giving the historic garments a contemporary staging that underscores the throughline between then and now. It is a show that rewards close looking at craftsmanship — hand embroidery, frog closures, and dye techniques — as much as it does thinking about dress as a form of quiet self-assertion for Chinese and Chinese American women across a century of dramatic change.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

shows.title: Danse Macabre: Death in Print from Durer to Dix
shows.description:
Skeletons have been dancing through European printmaking since the 14th century, and this focused installation of works on paper follows that morbid, oddly playful tradition from early woodcuts up through the German Expressionists working in the shadow of World War I. The danse macabre motif — Death leading figures from every social rank in a mocking procession — gave printmakers a shorthand for mortality that could be both comic and genuinely unsettling.

Drawn entirely from LACMA's collection, the prints here span roughly four centuries, letting you watch how the same essential image — the grinning skeleton, the hourglass, the personification of Death as a dance partner nobody can refuse — gets reinvented by artists responding to plague, war, and industrial-scale violence. It's a compact but pointed show, best suited to visitors who like their art history with a little bit of gallows humor.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

shows.title: Alfonso Gonzalez Jr.: In Between Stops
shows.description:
Twelve painted benches line LACMA's Kendall Concourse, each one designed by Alfonso Gonzalez Jr., a second-generation sign painter who learned rotulismo mexicano — the tradition of hand-lettered Mexican signage — from his father's shop. Instead of the ads you'd normally find on a bus bench, Gonzalez's panels carry personal messages, community references, and occasional nods to LACMA's own collection and history, turning a piece of street furniture into a small billboard for ideas that have nothing to do with selling anything.

The project sits at the intersection of fine art and vernacular craft, continuing a lineage of Los Angeles artists who've used the city's public infrastructure — benches, murals, storefronts — as exhibition space. It's a free, outdoor, easy-to-miss show that rewards visitors who slow down on their way between LACMA's buildings.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

shows.title: Ecce Artifex
shows.description:
Michael Flechtner has spent decades pushing neon past its signage roots into full sculptural territory, and this survey at the Museum of Neon Art gathers work spanning that career. Flechtner came up learning the trade in a six-week bending class in Kansas before moving to Los Angeles to work commercial neon by day and his own sculptures by night, and that hybrid background shows in the work: pieces that use the vocabulary of signage — bent glass tubing, buzzing color, graphic punch — but bend it toward visual puns and conceptual play rather than advertising.

The show's title, "Ecce Artifex" ("Behold the Craftsman"), answers his 1991 MONA solo debut "Ecce Signum" ("Behold the Sign"), and the pairing frames this as a kind of career-spanning victory lap for an artist who has quietly shaped how the medium is treated as art rather than commerce. Flechtner is also the fabricator behind neon elements in works by artists like Bruce Nauman, Doug Aitken, and Betye Saar, so this is also a rare chance to see his own authorial voice front and center rather than in service of someone else's piece.

Flechtner's show anchors the museum's current run of exhibitions and is worth catching before it closes in late September.

shows.title: Collecting Impressionism at LACMA
shows.description:
This is less a straightforward Impressionism show than a behind-the-scenes look at how a museum's identity gets built. It traces how paintings by Degas, Pissarro, and their contemporaries entered LACMA's collection through the taste and generosity of specific Hollywood-era donors and collectors, and asks why French Impressionism in particular has come to stand in for an entire late-19th-century visual culture that actually included printmaking, photography, fashion, and design.

The paintings themselves — landscapes, portraits, urban scenes — are the draw, but the real subject is collecting as an act of cultural self-definition: how a young museum in a young city used European "taste" to legitimize itself, and how that history is now being examined rather than simply celebrated. Anyone interested in provenance, philanthropy, and the politics of museum-building will find plenty to chew on here alongside the pretty pictures.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

shows.title: Deep Cuts: Block Printing Across Cultures
shows.description:
Block printing might be the oldest way humans figured out how to make the same image over and over, and this sprawling survey — more than 150 objects from Asia, Europe, and the Americas — treats it as both an art form and a communication technology. Patterned Indian textiles sit alongside illustrated Kelmscott Press books, German Expressionist woodcuts, and the razor-sharp contemporary prints of Christiane Baumgartner, tracing a single technique across wildly different cultures and centuries.

A section built with the Los Angeles textile studio Block Shop brings the story into the present, showing how a centuries-old process still has working artists and designers finding new uses for it. It's a show built for close looking — the pleasure here is in noticing how a carved block, whether cutting fabric patterns or fine art editions, keeps generating new visual possibilities out of a very old constraint. Note that this is in its final month, closing September 13.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

shows.title: Every Minute Is History: Five Views of Los Angeles
shows.artist: Laura Aguilar, Reynaldo Rivera, George Rodriguez, Patssi Valdez, Ricardo Valverde
shows.description:
Five photographers who worked in and around Los Angeles's Chicano/a communities anchor this survey, each pulling the camera toward a different corner of everyday life — Laura Aguilar's frank, body-conscious self-portraiture and documentary work with queer Latina communities, Reynaldo Rivera's nightlife and drag-bar portraits, George Rodriguez's photojournalism spanning music, sports and civil-rights history, Patssi Valdez's staged, theatrical tableaux rooted in her work with the group Asco, and Ricardo Valverde's hand-colored, experimental prints that fuse documentary and fine-art impulses.

What ties the five together is less a shared style than a shared refusal to let Chicano/a Los Angeles be photographed only from the outside. Aguilar and Valverde in particular pushed printing and color into expressive, sometimes surreal territory, while Rivera and Rodriguez worked closer to classic documentary and press photography. Seen together, the works trace roughly four decades of the city's visual history through a lens rarely centered in mainstream photography surveys.

The show opens alongside a companion exhibition of Mexican photography, and the pairing is intentional: both examine how a camera can hold a community's memory as much as its image. It's a strong, tightly focused two-gallery visit if you catch them together.

shows.title: Instante/revelación: Moments in Mexican Photography
shows.artist: Manuel Álvarez Bravo, Lola Álvarez Bravo, Manuel Carrillo, Antonio Reynoso, Héctor García, Mariana Yampolsky, Rodrigo Moya, Pedro Meyer, Graciela Iturbide, Yolanda Andrade, Pablo Ortiz Monasterio, Cecilia Salcedo Méndez, Flor Garduño
shows.description:
Nearly a century of Mexican photography, told through thirteen photographers whose work moves from the socially engaged modernism of Manuel and Lola Álvarez Bravo in the late 1920s and '30s through to the more conceptual, documentary-adjacent practices of figures like Graciela Iturbide and Pablo Ortiz Monasterio decades later. The pictures come almost entirely from a single source — a twenty-five-year run of gifts to the Getty from collectors Daniel Greenberg and Susan Steinhauser — which gives the show an unusually coherent backbone even as it ranges across generations and approaches.

The exhibition borrows its structure from Octavio Paz's 1982 book "Instante y revelación," which paired his poetry with Álvarez Bravo's photographs; here the galleries are organized around lines from a related Paz poem, using the poet's language as a loose armature for grouping the images rather than a strict chronology. Expect the recognizable high points of Mexican modernist photography alongside less-familiar later work, including Iturbide's color studies and Ortiz Monasterio's more recent digital-era photographs.

It's being shown deliberately in tandem with "Every Minute Is History," the Getty's concurrent survey of Chicano/a photographers in Los Angeles, and the two together make an argument about the visual dialogue between Mexico City and LA that's worth taking in as a pair.

shows.title: Lost. Found. Returned.
shows.description:
A small, focused provenance-research exhibition built around a single drawing: a nude study by the German Symbolist Otto Greiner, acquired by Dresden's Kupferstich-Kabinett in 1894 and marked "lost" after the Second World War before turning up, decades later, in the Getty Research Institute's own holdings. Rather than presenting a broad survey, the show walks through the detective work — archival sleuthing, condition and provenance clues — that let researchers trace the drawing's wartime disappearance and confirm its identity ahead of its return to Germany.

It's a quieter show than the Getty's big loan exhibitions, but it's a genuinely interesting look at how provenance research actually works, useful for anyone curious about the mechanics of restitution rather than just its headlines.

shows.title: Stendahl's World: Marketing Ancient Mexico and Modern Art in Los Angeles
shows.description:
Drawn from the Getty Research Institute's Stendahl Art Galleries archive, this show is a portrait of a single, unusually influential Los Angeles dealer rather than of any one artist. Earl Stendahl spent decades selling California Impressionism and introducing European modernists like Diego Rivera, Marc Chagall and Picasso to Southern California buyers before pivoting, in the mid-1930s, to marketing pre-Hispanic Mexican antiquities — a shift that reshaped the market for ancient American art on the West Coast.

The material here is archival rather than art-historical in the usual sense: photographs, gallery correspondence, sales records and publicity materials that show how Stendahl built demand through traveling shows, department-store tie-ins, celebrity collectors and even Hollywood product placement. The exhibition doesn't shy from the uglier consequences of that marketing success, noting the looting of Mexican archaeological sites that accompanied the boom in demand he helped create.

It's less a visual spectacle than a case study in taste-making, useful for anyone interested in how the market for "ancient" art gets built by very modern hands.

shows.title: The Making of a Medieval Manuscript
shows.description:
A process-focused show pulled from the Getty's own manuscript holdings, walking through the four stages that went into producing a book by hand in pre-modern Europe: preparing animal skin into parchment, then writing, painting and binding it. Rather than organizing around a single theme or artist, the curators use roughly a dozen manuscripts — including biblical and Qur'anic pages worked in tempera, gold leaf and ink — to illustrate each technical stage in turn.

It's a good primer for anyone who loves illuminated manuscripts but has never quite understood how the physical objects were actually made, with close attention paid to material and craft rather than iconography alone.

shows.title: Five Centuries of Works on Paper: The Grunwald Center at 70, Part II
shows.description:
The second half of a two-part anniversary show marking seventy years of UCLA's Grunwald Center for the Graphic Arts, one of the country's major repositories of prints, drawings, photographs and artists' books. Housed at the Hammer since 1994, the collection began with a 1956 gift from Los Angeles collector Fred Grunwald and has grown into a holding of more than 45,000 works spanning the Renaissance to the present.

This installment leans into that range: Dürer woodcuts and Piranesi etchings sit alongside Hiroshige's Edo-period landscapes, Degas and Manet prints, and a run of twentieth-century material that includes Käthe Kollwitz, Egon Schiele, Picasso and Matisse. The photography side of the collection gets real attention too, with Ansel Adams and Imogen Cunningham running into more conceptually driven work by Robert Heinecken, James Welling and Catherine Opie. Contemporary names — Julie Mehretu, James Turrell, Alison Saar, Kara Walker — round out the picture, making the point that the Grunwald's holdings didn't stop accumulating at some tasteful historical cutoff.

It's a survey show in the best sense: less an argument than an occasion to look closely at seventy-plus individual objects, many of them rarely on view, drawn entirely from a single institution's collection.

shows.title: Inventing America: The Comic Book Revolution
shows.description:
This sprawling survey traces the American comic book from its Depression-era beginnings through the turn of the millennium, using original art, vintage covers, and rare production artifacts to show how a disposable pulp medium became a mirror for the national psyche. The show leans hard on the fact that so many of the medium's founding artists and writers were immigrants and outsiders — many of them Jewish — whose own experience of displacement and reinvention shaped the archetypes (the orphaned alien who becomes a savior, the mild-mannered outcast with a secret power) that are now global shorthand for American myth-making.

Expect to see the medium's marquee names — Superman, Wonder Woman, Captain America, Spider-Man, Black Panther, Archie, the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles — alongside pencil roughs and character studies that reveal the working process behind the finished page. The installation photos show gallery walls given over to mural-scale blow-ups of classic covers, a reminder that these images functioned as genuinely mass culture long before "graphic novel" became a respectable term.

Rather than a nostalgia trip, the exhibition frames comics as historical documents: stand-ins for anxieties about war, civil rights, and the changing shape of American identity across six decades. It's a good pick for anyone who grew up on these characters and wants the fuller, stranger story behind their creation, and it runs long enough (through February 2027) that there's no rush to catch it.

shows.title: A Palace in Time
shows.description:
Two Los Angeles painters and life partners share a gallery for an exhibition built around the idea of the Sabbath as, in Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel's phrase, "a palace in time." Robert Russell contributes softly rendered still lifes of Jewish ritual objects — Kiddush cups, yahrzeit candles — painted with a hazy, almost dissolving touch that turns ordinary domestic objects into vessels of memory and quiet loss.
