Lisa Edelstein works from her own family photo archive, reconstructing scenes of 1970s suburban New Jersey Jewish life: crowded multigenerational gatherings, patterned wallpaper and furniture, small unposed moments of touch and affection. Her palette and subject matter read as warmer and more anecdotal than Russell's, and the pairing of the two bodies of work sets an intimate, personal register against a more symbolic, object-based one.

Together the two painters build a meditation on ritual, domestic time, and inherited memory — what gets held onto materially versus what only survives as recollection. It's a modestly scaled, human-sized show, and it closes the same week as the museum's punk exhibition, so it's worth pairing on one visit.

shows.title: Mountain Spirits: Rice and Indigeneity in the Northern Luzon Highlands, Philippines
shows.dates_note: Venue page gives the closing only as "January, 2027" with no specific day; saved as Jan 31, 2027 pending confirmation.
shows.description:
This exhibition looks at the Ifugao people of the northern Luzon highlands in the Philippines, whose terraced rice fields — carved into mountainsides over centuries and recognized by UNESCO — are as much spiritual infrastructure as agricultural engineering. Rather than treating the terraces as a scenic backdrop, the show insists they're a living, working culture: a place where farming, ritual, and kinship are inseparable.

The galleries bring together carved guardian figures, ritual bowls, woven textiles, and traditional farming tools alongside video and soundscape installations that situate the objects in their landscape and social context. It's a materials-rich show that rewards slow looking — the carvings especially carry the kind of formal power that made Philippine highland sculpture influential well beyond its region.

What makes this show worth the trip is its refusal to freeze Ifugao culture in the past tense: the framing throughout is that these terraces and traditions are ongoing, not museum relics, and the video work by Paul Connor reinforces that sense of a still-living practice. Paired with the Fowler's other current exhibitions on textile monuments and African art provenance, it rounds out a strong season on land, memory, and material culture.

shows.title: Belongings: Changing Hands and Shifting Meanings in African Arts
shows.description:
Most museum displays of African art present objects at the moment of their making, explaining how a mask or figure was meant to be used within its originating community. This show does something different: it tracks what happened to these objects afterward — the string of hands, markets, and meanings they passed through on the way from Africa to a Los Angeles museum vitrine.

Organized around four stages of an object's journey — from original owners, to colonial-era acquisition, to the European secondary market, to arrival at the Fowler — the exhibition uses carved masks, figures, and other historical African works as case studies in the politics of collecting. A featured Bamileke Tsesah mask from Cameroon, gifted via the Wellcome Trust, stands as a good example of the kind of object under scrutiny here: beautifully carved, but carrying a provenance far more tangled than a simple label usually admits.

The show is explicitly an argument about museum authority — it wants visitors to understand that no wall text is the final word, and that objects "contain multitudes" as they move between owners and contexts. That makes it a useful, slightly uncomfortable companion piece to more celebratory African-art displays, and a good entry point for anyone curious about restitution debates playing out at museums across the US and Europe right now.

shows.title: Nurtured Flames: The Medicine of Fire
shows.artist: joel garcia, River Garza, Ishi Glinsky, Artemiza (Ciara Green), Adrienne Kinsella, Kenneth Lopez, Emma Robbins, Kimberly Robertson, Aanii Tate, Isaac Michael Ybarra, Alexandria Ybarra
shows.description:
Organized with Meztli Projects, an Indigenous arts and culture collaborative, this exhibition brings together eleven Indigenous artists working across generations to rethink fire — not as disaster or destruction, but as a tool of stewardship long used by Indigenous communities for land care, renewal, and cultural continuity. The work was developed collaboratively, with artists trading ideas and feedback with each other and with tribal elders and culture bearers over the course of the project.

Given the exhibition's opening arrives just over a year and a half after the Eaton Fire tore through nearby Altadena, the show's reframing of fire as something other than pure catastrophe feels pointed without being didactic. Expect a range of media — painting, sculpture, and mixed-media work grounded in specific cultural practices rather than a single unified style, since the artists come from distinct communities and generations.

The exhibition runs in the Armory's Caldwell Gallery through mid-January 2027, giving it an unusually long run for a Pasadena nonprofit space, and reflects the Armory's continued commitment to Indigenous-led curatorial projects.

shows.title: "This Land Is ..." Exhibition
shows.description:
Timed to the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, this sprawling group exhibition uses the Huntington's own library, art, and botanical holdings to ask what "land" has meant in the American imagination — as property, as promise, as home, and as a site of dispossession. The show's title nods to Woody Guthrie's "This Land Is Your Land," and the trailing ellipsis is doing real work: everything here complicates the anthem's easy claim.

The material ranges wildly, from an early printed copy of the Declaration itself and a George Washington land grant to a Langston Hughes poem and a well-worn guitar, alongside historical photographs, maps, and artwork that trace westward expansion, Indigenous displacement, and the country's contested relationship to its own territory. It's less a single argument than a layered conversation, moving from the Atlantic coast to the Pacific and from the colonial period into the present.

It's an ambitious, research-heavy show best suited to visitors happy to slow down and read; the payoff is a far more textured picture of American land history than the marketing bunting around most 250th-anniversary programming tends to offer.

venue.name: The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens

shows.title: (Be)Spoken: Poems from Our Asian American Voices
shows.description:
Spoken word gets a gallery treatment in this show co-curated by rapper and poet Jason Chu, who assembled seven voices from LA's Asian American poetry and performance scene — Tanzila "Taz" Ahmed, arianna lady basco, Emdash, Sun Luu, Michelle Myers, STEADY, and Catzie Vilayphonh. Rather than simply mount text on the wall, the museum translates their poems into installation, photography, and staged imagery, treating performance as a visual medium as much as a verbal one.

The result is less a literary archive than an immersive listening room: visitors move through pieces that foreground identity, resilience, and community across generations of Chinese American and broader AAPI experience. It's a fitting complement to CAM's historical galleries next door, pulling the museum's mission — preserving Chinese American history — into the present tense of contemporary voice and protest poetry.

Closing September 6, this is a last chance to catch a show that treats poetry as a communal, embodied act rather than a page-bound one.

shows.title: We Belong Here
shows.description:
We Belong Here turns the exterior walls of LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes into a rotating outdoor gallery of projections and neon signage, made in coordination with four other Los Angeles institutions — the California Community Foundation, JANM, MOLAA, and SPARC — each showing its own selection on its own building. The work leans hard into protest graphics: Lalo Alcaraz, Ernesto Yerena Montejano, Man One, and others contribute images that speak directly to immigration enforcement, detention, and the experience of being undocumented in this political moment.

It's public art in the most literal sense — visible from the street after dark, free to encounter without a ticket — and it functions as a companion piece to CCF's "Am I Next" campaign against silence in the face of ICE activity in Los Angeles. Content shifts by site, so LA Plaza's Main Street-facing selection is only part of a citywide project, but the images shown here (including Alcaraz's recurring "ICE Out of LA" motif) are pointed, current, and unambiguous about whose side the institution is on.

Given the museum's mission as a keeper of Latino LA history, the piece reads as an extension of its core work rather than a departure — using its own walls to make a case for who the city belongs to.

venue.name: LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes

shows.title: Sanctified Steel
shows.description:
Jacqueline Valenzuela paints the garage as a kind of chapel. Her first solo show with Craig Krull Gallery gathers densely worked panels — built up from oil and automotive paint, faux fur, jeweled and pompom trim, gold leaf, and even found personal objects like votive candles — that frame lowrider culture in the visual language of Catholic devotion. Many pieces borrow the shape of the nicho, the small shadow-box altar used to honor saints and lost loved ones, and repurpose it to hold portraits of cars, women, and family memory instead.

Valenzuela, who grew up in East Los Angeles and has spent years working alongside painters and fabricators in an auto body shop, treats restoration and customization as acts of care and inheritance rather than mere craft. Recurring appearances of the Virgen de Guadalupe tie the individual stories in the show — a red Corvair remembered with marigolds and candlelight, a friend's crudely spray-painted car in "Just Like Candy" — to a larger tradition of veneration and cultural pride, including the reclaimed concept of rasquachismo, making the most of what's at hand.

The result is a body of work that insists lowrider culture and fine-art materials belong in the same sentence: chrome-shop bravado rendered with the patience and symbolism of an altarpiece. It's a striking, tactile show, heavy with texture and personal narrative, and a strong introduction to an artist building a wider reputation for centering women's experience within a famously male-coded car culture.
shows.reception: Saturday, September 12, 4-6pm (in conjunction with Bergamot Station's Fall Open House); Artist Talk Saturday, September 19, 11am

shows.title: Walking Venice
shows.description:
Craig Krull, better known in Los Angeles as a gallerist, turns his own camera on the neighborhood that raised him. Walking Venice collects small-format archival pigment prints made during meandering daily walks he began during the pandemic — a return to the alleys, canals, and boardwalk he first roamed as a kid in the early 1970s and later lived beside as a young gallery hand in the 1980s.

The pictures favor palimpsest and decay over postcard landmarks: piles of discarded furniture and street debris arranged, almost sculpturally, by the people who live among them; architectural fragments; the funky, unbothered texture of alleys like Speedway that gentrification hasn't managed to scrub clean. Krull cites the deliberate, meditative walking-as-art practices of Richard Long and Roger Ackling as a touchstone, and the photographs — intimate, often just 4x5 inches printed onto larger sheets — read like a diary of attention rather than a survey of sights.

At the center of the gallery Krull has installed Memento, a tower of mismatched concrete breeze blocks planted with sweet alyssum — a quiet sculptural coda to a show that's ultimately about one person's decades-long, still-unfolding relationship with a single square mile of Los Angeles.
shows.reception: Saturday, September 12, 4-6pm (in conjunction with Bergamot Station's Fall Open House); Artist Talk Saturday, September 19, 11am

shows.title: Rainbows, Sponges, Flies, and Spoons
shows.description:
SUPERFLEX, the Danish collective founded in 1993 by Jakob Fenger, Bjørnstjerne Christiansen, and Rasmus Rosengren Nielsen, brings three decades of work into R.M. Schindler's 1922 Kings Road house — itself an experiment in communal living, which gives the show an unusually direct dialogue with its site. Rather than one installation, the exhibition splits into several discrete bodies of work, each given its own room: an early lightbox photograph of spoons arranged in a circle, mirrored rainbow photographs that create an artificial, uncanny symmetry, a ceramic sponge sculpture proposed as a new architectural form, and a hyper-precise sculptural tableau of two flies staring at each other over a glass of water.

The connecting thread is SUPERFLEX's long-running interest in systems — ecological, architectural, social — approached through humor and quiet estrangement rather than didacticism. That interest has taken the collective everywhere from energy infrastructure and public parks (their Superkilen project in Copenhagen) to museum walls at Tate Modern and MoMA, and biennials from Venice to Sharjah.

Seeing this work inside the Schindler House is the real draw: a building designed to hold both collective and private life becomes the backdrop for objects that keep splitting the difference between the natural and the artificial, the individual and the shared. It's a tightly focused show rather than a survey, which suits the intimate scale of the house itself.

venue.name: MAK Center for Art and Architecture — Schindler House

shows.title: ReVOlt 1680/2180: Sirens & Sikas
shows.description:
Cochiti Pueblo artist Virgil Ortiz turns the history of the 1680 Pueblo Revolt into speculative fiction, imagining a future in which the rebels who drove Spanish colonizers from Puebloan land have interstellar allies. The exhibition presents Ortiz's sculptural figures — armored "Sirens," alien "artificers," and other characters rendered in the artist's distinctive blend of traditional Cochiti pottery techniques and sci-fi costuming — as part of an ongoing multi-chapter narrative he calls ReVOlt 1680/2180.

It's a sharp piece of world-building: Ortiz treats Po'pay's historic victory as the seed of an alternate timeline, using genre tropes (space travel, armor, insurgent technology) to keep a 340-year-old act of resistance alive as something forward-looking rather than archival. The figures are theatrical and highly detailed, closer to costume design and character concept art than to conventional ceramic sculpture.

The show is part of the Autry's larger Future Imaginaries: Indigenous Art, Fashion, Technology initiative and was produced under the PST ART: Art & Science Collide umbrella, so it sits at the intersection of contemporary Native art, fashion, and speculative design. Worth catching before it closes in early October — this run has been up since 2024 and is nearing the end of its extended stay at the museum.

venue.name: Autry Museum of the American West

shows.title: LIGHT
shows.description:
"LIGHT" is one of TAG's regular themed group shows, gathering member artists of this longtime Wilshire Boulevard artists' collective around a single loose prompt — in this case light itself, in whatever medium or approach each participant chooses. TAG has run these seasonal theme shows for years (past editions have tackled water, fire, earth and force & energy), and they function as a kind of snapshot of the collective's range: painters, photographers and mixed-media artists all responding independently to the same word.

Because TAG is an artist-run cooperative rather than a commercial gallery with a single curatorial voice, these group shows tend to be eclectic by design — expect a wide swing in style and subject rather than a tightly argued thesis. That variety is part of the draw: it's a good way to get a broad sample of what a working, membership-based Los Angeles gallery looks like right now, alongside TAG's concurrent solo presentations in its adjoining project rooms.

shows.title: Eyes on the World / Americana Cookie Jar Icons
shows.description:
This paired presentation splits TAG's project rooms between two very different bodies of work. Noah Hass-Cohen's "Eyes on the World" is a ceramic sculpture practice, while Amit Cohen's "Americana Cookie Jar Icons" repurposes the kitschy, nostalgic form of the mid-century cookie jar as a vehicle for commentary on American pop iconography — taking a domestic collectible object and pushing it toward something more pointed and art-historically self-aware.

Pairing a sculptor working in clay with an artist reworking a specific vernacular ceramic form makes for a natural conversation about material, craft history and kitsch, even though the two practices arrived at the material from different directions. It's a good entry point for anyone interested in how contemporary artists are re-engaging with ceramics and "low" collectible forms rather than treating them as decorative background.

This is one part of TAG's broader September calendar of concurrent solo and group shows across the gallery's several rooms, running alongside the group show "LIGHT."

shows.title: Dale Sizer: Mini Show
shows.description:
Dale Sizer's four-painting mini-show at Copro turns Old Hollywood into pulp-glamour icon painting: Barbara Payton, Gene Tierney, Marilyn Monroe and a trio of "Valley of the Dolls" stars (Sharon Tate, Barbara Parkins, Patty Duke) get the mixed-media, acrylic-on-canvas treatment, their faces rendered with the graphic punch of vintage movie-poster art.

Sizer's background is exactly what you'd guess from the work — decades as an illustrator and animation background painter for studios including Disney, Warner Bros. and 20th Century Fox, plus record-cover and ad work for major labels and brands. That commercial-art fluency shows in how cleanly these portraits read: bold, poster-ready compositions built for maximum star-power at a glance, tinged with the melancholy that tends to follow stories about doomed Hollywood starlets.

It's a small, focused hang running alongside Mook Simpson's "America Dreaming" and Helena Reis's "Duskborn" in Copro's August rotation.

shows.title: From Delicate to Dynamic
shows.dates_note: Venue site gives no exact opening date; closing confirmed by its calendar entry "Closing of 'From Delicate to Dynamic'" on 9/12/2026. Start date estimated from show being third in a run of exhibitions this year — treat as approximate.
shows.description:
Curator Dale Youngman has put together a group survey of abstraction that deliberately avoids picking a side in the old quiet-versus-loud debate. The checklist runs from spare, meditative compositions to thickly worked, high-contrast pieces built on color and gesture, and the point seems to be showing visitors how much territory the word "abstract" actually covers.

Seventeen artists are in the mix, including Bill Sherwood, Clara Berta, Cody Bayne, DAK (David A. Knudsen), Gil Tepper, Lina Kogan, and Varoujan Hovakimyan, giving the show enough range that no single hand or palette dominates. The gallery has paired the exhibition with two artist panels — one on tool-driven process, another on whether abstract work can carry narrative — which suggests the curatorial interest here is as much in method as in finished surface.

Blue & The Muse is a small Little Tokyo-adjacent space, and shows like this one are exactly its niche: accessible entry points into abstraction for a general audience, without the market-driven throat-clearing of a blue-chip gallery.

shows.title: ADRIAN: Designing Hollywood, Dressing America
shows.description:
Gilbert Adrian was the costume designer who built MGM's glamour machine in the 1930s and '40s, and this exhibition is a chance to see just how much engineering went into that glamour up close. The ASU FIDM Museum is pulling more than fifty ensembles and accessories from its own deep costume-history collection, supplemented by loans from private collectors, to trace Adrian's path from Hollywood soundstage to his own Wilshire Boulevard couture salon.

What made Adrian's work so enduring wasn't just spectacle — it was structural. His sharp shoulders and bias-cut gowns for stars like Joan Crawford and Jean Harlow reshaped what American ready-to-wear looked like once department stores started knocking off his silhouettes nationwide. The show promises pieces connected to more than 200 film productions, including costumes tied to The Wizard of Oz, alongside sketches and ephemera that show the design process behind the finished garments.

For a museum with free admission and no advance booking, this is a rare opportunity to get close to Golden Age costume design outside a film archive. Fashion history and film history collide here, and the installation itself — mannequins under the museum's soft gallery light — is worth the trip even before you start reading the wall text.

venue.name: ASU FIDM Museum
venue.address_detail: Museum entrance on ground floor, ASU California Center Grand
hours: Wed - Sat 10:00am to 5:00pm (open only during exhibitions)

shows.title: The Not-So-Fine Art Show: The Minds Behind the Magic of Animation Art
shows.description:
Animation studio Titmouse teams up with FAB LA Gallery for a group show devoted to the artists who draw, design, and direct the characters that populate contemporary cartoons and pop culture. Rather than treating animation art as illustration on the side, the exhibition presents original cels, character studies, and standalone canvases as the main event, putting veteran animation-industry names alongside a newer generation of visual artists working in the same idiom.

The show fits naturally into FAB LA's identity as a pop-culture-facing gallery inside the landmark Fine Arts Building on 7th Street: owner Kii Arens has spent decades commissioning music-driven pop imagery for artists from The Rolling Stones to Lady Gaga, and this exhibition extends that sensibility into animation, treating cartoon design as a legitimate branch of contemporary visual art rather than mere merchandise.

Expect a loose, high-energy hang of character portraits, storyboards-turned-artworks, and brightly colored studio pieces, the kind of show built for browsing and buying rather than austere contemplation. It's a good pick for anyone curious about the visual culture behind the animated shows and films that shape mainstream imagination, presented in a gorgeously tiled Romanesque Revival lobby that is itself worth the visit.

venue.name: FAB LA Gallery
hours: Mon - Fri 9:00am to 6:00pm (lobby); private viewings by appointment

shows.title: Jiroft: Seven Valleys in Bloom
shows.description:
Hiva Alizadeh takes her title from Jiroft, the southeastern Iranian archaeological site whose Bronze Age carved chlorite vessels rank among the oldest surviving examples of figurative art from the Iranian plateau. Working across painting and mixed media, Alizadeh translates that ancient visual vocabulary — spiraling florals, animal-headed motifs, dense surface patterning — into a contemporary register, treating the millennia-old carvings less as archaeology than as a living design language still available to draw from.

The paintings on view lean into saturated color and stylized botanical forms, suggesting gardens that are as much invented as remembered. There's a diaristic, almost devotional quality to the repetition of blooms and vines across the canvases, as if the artist is working through a personal iconography built from a shared cultural memory rather than direct observation.

The show is a fitting anchor: it treats a deep national history not as a fixed heritage to be illustrated but as material to be reactivated in paint. It's worth seeing alongside the two solo shows opening the same week at Gallery One, which round out a fuller picture of how different Iranian-American women artists are handling questions of memory, myth, and inheritance right now.

shows.title: Storyless
shows.description:
Anali Taherian's Storyless is a brief, tightly wound solo presentation in the gallery's smaller Gallery One space — on view for just two weeks, which makes it feel more like a pointed statement than a survey. The title suggests a deliberate refusal of narrative, and the works lean into ambiguity: fragmented compositions and imagery that resist being read as illustration of any single event or memory.

There's a quietness to the installation that plays against the more maximalist, pattern-driven work showing concurrently in the Main Gallery. Taherian seems more interested in withholding than accumulating — leaving gaps in the picture plane, letting color and mark stand in for whatever story isn't being told.

Worth a visit if you're already coming for the Hiva Alizadeh show next door; the two exhibitions make an interesting pair, one insisting on inherited pattern and myth, the other stripping narrative away almost entirely.

shows.title: Whispers: Women, Animals and Chimeras
shows.description:
Elika Hedayat's Whispers gathers a menagerie of hybrid figures — women fused with animals, chimeric bodies that slip between the human and the mythic — into what reads as a meditation on femininity refracted through folklore. The imagery draws on a long tradition of composite creatures in Persian and broader Middle Eastern storytelling, where animal-headed women and shape-shifting bodies carry warnings, protections, and desires that couldn't be spoken plainly.

Rendered with a soft, almost illustrative touch, the works feel intimate rather than monumental — more whispered confidences than declarations, true to the title. It's the longest-running of the three shows the gallery opens this week, giving it room to be the anchor exhibition through much of September and into October.

Seen together with Hiva Alizadeh's botanical abstractions and Anali Taherian's spare Storyless, Hedayat's chimeras complete a loose trilogy of shows built around inherited image-worlds — pattern, silence, and myth — all filtered through women's perspectives.

shows.title: Creative Continuities: Family, Pride, and Community in Native Art
shows.artist: John Pepion, Brocade Stops Black Eagle, Jessa Rae Growing Thunder
shows.description:
Three contemporary Plains Indian artists — Blackfeet painter John Pepion, Crow (Apsáalooke) artist Brocade Stops Black Eagle, and Dakota/Nakoda beadworker Jessa Rae Growing Thunder — were invited to curate sections of the Autry's Native American collection through their own cultural lenses. Rather than a conventional survey of historic objects, the show pairs beadwork, garments, and regalia made by past generations with new works and commentary from these three "culture bearers," organized around the ideas of Knowing, Creating, and Transference.

The result is a conversation across time: a 19th-century Miniconjou Lakota pipe bag or a Crow beaded vest sits alongside contemporary pieces like Pepion's ink-on-antique-map painting Our Land, making the case that Plains Native art-making is a living, continuous practice rather than a closed chapter of history. A Blackfeet tipi, fully assembled inside the gallery, anchors the installation and comes with its own audio guide.

This is one of the more thoughtfully collaborative exhibitions in the Autry's collection galleries — instead of anthropologists or curators speaking for Native material culture, the artists whose communities made these objects get to frame their meaning directly. It runs for over a year and a half, so there's no rush, but it rewards a slow look at beadwork and garment craftsmanship that's easy to walk past on autopilot.

venue.name: Autry Museum of the American West

shows.title: The Long Way Home
shows.description:
Billed as a "mini solo exhibition," Susie Ketchum's The Long Way Home fills La Luz de Jesus's smaller gallery wall with dense, symbol-laden imagery — a mask trailing dangling skulls, a red flower rendered with fetishistic precision, a tree-woman hybrid figure — that fits comfortably within the gallery's decades-long identity as ground zero for Pop Surrealism and lowbrow art.

The pieces work in a register somewhere between illustration and folk-horror talisman: skulls, embers, and shedding skin recur as motifs, suggesting a loose narrative of transformation, protection, and reckoning with mortality that runs through the small body of work. Ketchum's rendering is tight and graphic, closer to tattoo flash or album art than academic painting, which suits the show's compact, charm-like scale.

Opening the same first-Friday night as Wini Brewer's solo show next door in the gallery, The Long Way Home is a good entry point for anyone curious about the darker, more occult-inflected end of the lowbrow tradition La Luz de Jesus helped define.

shows.title: Aesthetic Strategies
shows.description:
Wini Brewer's solo show Aesthetic Strategies takes over La Luz de Jesus's main gallery for a run of new work that, per the artist's promotional material, leans into bold, graphic composition and a considered, almost design-driven approach to image-making — hence the exhibition's title.

La Luz de Jesus has spent forty years as the launching pad for pop-surrealist and lowbrow artists working outside the traditional gallery pipeline, and Brewer's inclusion in the September calendar continues that mission, putting a contemporary illustrator's sensibility on the walls of what is still one of the genre's most storied showcases.

Without a full install shot or checklist yet published, the show is best approached as a first-Friday discovery: it opens alongside Susie Ketchum's mini solo next door, giving visitors two very different, tightly-hung bodies of work to compare in one visit.

shows.title: Edmund Teske: On Olive Hill
shows.description:
Edmund Teske arrived at Olive Hill in 1943 as a young photographer who had studied under Frank Lloyd Wright at Taliesin, and this exhibition gathers his photographs of Hollyhock House during a formative, unstable moment in its history — the years before the site's major 1946 restoration, when the house was in visible disrepair. Aline Barnsdall invited Teske to live in a guest house on the property, giving him a darkroom and effectively making him an informal caretaker-in-residence.

The photographs on view document Wright's "California Romanza" in transition: sunlit courtyards and crumbling ornament, captured by an artist who described the place as sailing "with the clouds." Teske was known for double exposures and composite printing, techniques scholars have noted let him fold together different moments in time within a single frame — an approach especially suited to a building whose own history is one of decay, renewal, and reinvention.

All of the photographs were gifted to the City of Los Angeles by Michael and David Devine, and the show functions as a quiet historical counterpoint to the more polished, restored Hollyhock House visitors encounter today — a glimpse of the building's shabbier, more bohemian middle age, host to figures like Man Ray and John Lautner.

shows.title: One Last Group Show (untitled friends exhibition)
shows.artist: Kuma Enomoto, Marilyn Garcia, Filomena Leimone, Santiago Orellana, Lucia Penick, and Eloise Wong
shows.description:
This send-off show gathers six recent graduates of an LA arts high school who've spent years crossing paths at each other's shows, gigs, and film shoots — scoring one another's movies, photographing one another's bands, modeling one another's clothes. Painting, photography, animation, and mixed media all show up here, tied together less by a curatorial thesis than by the fact that everyone in the room has been each other's audience and collaborator for years.

This show captures that spirit at a bittersweet moment: several of the artists are leaving Los Angeles just as the show closes. Expect work that's rougher and more personal than a typical gallery show, dealing openly with community, heartbreak, and the anxiety of growing up in a hostile world, with a closing-night musical send-off from two of the artists' bands.

shows.title: Broken Sleeps
shows.description:
Fiona Connor has spent years making exacting, deadpan replicas of overlooked civic and social infrastructure — noticeboards, drinking fountains, storefront gates — objects whose surfaces carry the residue of public use. Broken Sleeps, her third solo show with Château Shatto, marks a turn in that practice: rather than faithfully reproducing an existing object down to its scars, these new sculptures are built through what the gallery describes as material translation, letting the source object loosen into something more poetic and less strictly documentary.

Connor's work has always lived in the gap between sculpture and readymade, asking viewers to look twice at things designed to be invisible. This show promises to push that inquiry further, trading precision-replica fidelity for a looser, more interpretive kind of object-making — a meaningful development for an artist whose reputation was built on exactness.

Given Connor's track record — her work has been included in major museum surveys and she is one of the gallery's longest-running artists — this is a show worth catching close to its opening, before word spreads.

shows.title: Ain't it Fun Always Being on the Run?
shows.description:
This group show, subtitled "Cole Dallas' Last Picture Show," gathers a loose crew of painters, sculptors, filmmakers and performers around designer Cole Dallas's own artisanal clothing label CD1974. Curated by Dallas together with Jordan Hubert, Mona Cesario, and Siena Soltis, it treats the gallery as a kind of backstage-meets-showroom, mixing garment-as-sculpture with more conventional studio work.

The roster — Charmont des Noir, T. Antonakis Kane, Luis Miguel Anaya, Wally Waliszewski, Hannah Baskin, Bella Stacia, and the collective Hot American Girls — spans painting, sculpture, and film, and the checklist is rounded out with live performance elements on select nights, keeping the exhibition from sitting still for its short two-and-a-half week run.

It's a good example of the scrappy, artist-driven programming that Art/Space 114 has built a reputation for in the Old Bank District: less a tidy thesis show than a snapshot of overlapping downtown LA social and creative circles, staged with real fashion-world flair.

shows.title: Board Choice
shows.description:
For Avenue 50 Studio's 25th year, the gallery hands curatorial control to its own Board of Directors: each current or emeritus board member picked one or two artists whose work they personally admire, and the result is stitched together into a single group show. It's less a thematic exhibition than a group portrait of the people who've kept this Highland Park nonprofit running for a quarter-century — their taste, their relationships, their advocacy.

Artists span photography (Leopoldo Peña's black-and-white silver gelatin prints of Southern California vernacular structures), painting (Frank Romero, a name closely tied to LA's Chicano art history), and printmaking and mixed media from a roster of Eastside-connected artists including Armando Brito, Roberto Gutierrez, and Alex Donis. Because selections were made by personal admiration rather than a single curatorial thesis, expect real range in medium and generation.

Avenue 50 has been a fixture of the Highland Park/Northeast LA arts community since 2000, championing Latinx, Chicanx, and other under-recognized local artists, and this show doubles as an informal history lesson in who has shaped that mission from the inside.

shows.title: Diving Into the Wreck
shows.description:
This is the first full career survey of Los Angeles artist Susan Silton, organized by the Blaffer Art Museum in Houston and traveling to LAMAG with over 150 works spanning four decades. Silton works across photography, video, audio, participatory installation, and text-based projects, and the survey format lets you trace recurring preoccupations — the body and voice, shifting perspective, printed multiples, and the construction of public memory — across very different media.

Highlights include the video-and-sound installation "Bursting in air," the archival stereoscope piece "Mutation #6" from her early 1990s series mutatis mutandis, and "Inside Out," a site-specific tarp-and-sandbag installation originally made for the Pasadena Museum of California Art. The show also debuts a new public project, "Civilized Voices," in which Silton has commissioned Los Angeles poets to write text for hand-painted billboards installed among the pine trees outside the gallery, echoing billboards Aline Barnsdall herself once erected on the site.

A centerpiece is the reactivation of "In everything there is the trace," a circular table of ten interlocking manual typewriters where visitors type — without ink — through Octavia Butler's "Parable of the Sower" over the course of the run, turning the gallery into a living, collective transcription project. Taken together, the show makes a strong case for Silton as an under-recognized figure in West Coast conceptual, feminist, and queer art history, and it's worth catching both for the archival material and for the participatory works that only exist while the show is open.

shows.title: Follow the Feather
shows.description:
GOBI's current show gives Ruoyi Shi a solo platform. "Follow the Feather" leans into the gallery's interest in objects that sit between art and function, and Shi's work continues that conversation between material, craft, and image.

Based on the installation photos, the show favors a light, airy hang with sculptural and wall-based pieces that play with fragility and motion, fitting the exhibition's avian title.

Catching "Follow the Feather" before it closes in late September is worthwhile for anyone interested in emerging sculpture and object-based practice.

shows.title: The American Road Trip
shows.description:
This juried group exhibition from the California Art Club gathers dozens of plein air and studio painters working in the club's signature traditional, representational style, all riffing on the great American road trip. Timed to the 250th anniversary of the United States and the 175th anniversary of California statehood, the show is less about cars than about the landscapes and roadside moments a cross-country drive turns up: lone cypresses on coastal highways, diner-adjacent gas stations, farm stands, mission-era trails, and river crossings rendered in oil, watercolor, pastel, and colored pencil.

The work ranges widely in subject and mood, from Cliff Barnes's weathered cypress on Pebble Beach's 17-Mile Drive to John Kosta's twilight view of the Los Angeles River and its Beaux-Arts bridges, to Sandy Delehanty's glowing watercolor of Sedona's red rocks. Many of the artists write short first-person notes about the specific place and moment behind each painting, giving the show the feel of a collective travelogue as much as a themed art exhibition.

It's a good entry point for anyone curious about the California Art Club's ongoing commitment to representational and plein air painting traditions that trace back over a century in Southern California, exhibited in the modest historic setting of the Old Mill gallery in San Marino.

shows.title: Carroll Dunham
shows.description:
Carroll Dunham has spent five decades building one of contemporary painting's most instantly recognizable vocabularies — biomorphic forms, cartoonish anatomy, and hot, unmixed color pushed to the edge of abstraction — and this show at Matthew Brown's Seward Street space brings a new body of paintings, including works from his ongoing "Sharing Space" series glimpsed in the gallery's promotional image.

Dunham emerged from the downtown New York scene of the 1980s and has remained one of the most influential painters of his generation for younger figurative and abstract painters alike; his work moves fluidly between grotesque comedy and formal rigor, often mining the human body — especially figures rendered with exaggerated, almost violent simplicity — for both humor and unease.

This is a rare opportunity to see a major senior American painter's new work on the West Coast.
